nodes.name: Domain notation
nodes.statement: We use $\dom{X}$ to denote the domain of random variable $X$ and $\dom{\mathbf{X}}$ to denote the Cartesian product of the domains of all the variables in set $\mathbf{X}$, i.e., $\prod_{X\in \mathbf{X}} \dom{X}$.

nodes.name: Integer interval notation
nodes.statement: For integer numbers $a\leq b$, we use $[a:b]$ to denote $\{a,a+1,\cdots,b\}$.

nodes.name: Causal DAG with observed and unobserved variables
nodes.statement: Suppose $\mathcal{G}=(\mathbf{V} \cup \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{E})$ is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) over vertex set $\mathbf{V} \cup \mathbf{U}$, where $\mathbf{V}$ and $\mathbf{U}$ represent the set of observed and unobserved variables, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: G is a DAG over observed variables V and unobserved variables U.

nodes.name: Parent and child
nodes.statement: For each edge $(X, Y)\in \mathbf{E}$, $X$ is called a parent of $Y$, and $Y$ is called a child of $X$.

nodes.name: Ancestor
nodes.statement:
Vertex $X$ is an ancestor of $Y$ in $\mathcal{G}$ if a directed path exists from $X$ to $Y$ in $\mathcal{G}$.
        Note that $X$ is an ancestor of itself.
differentia: a directed path exists from $X$ to $Y$ in $\mathcal{G}$

nodes.name: Parent, child and ancestor set notation
nodes.statement:
$\Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}}$, $\Ch{X}{\mathcal{G}}$, and $\Anc{X}{\mathcal{G}}$ denote the set of parents, children, and ancestors of $X$ in $\mathcal{G}$, respectively.
        These notations are also used for a set of vertices. 
        In this case, they refer to the union over the set elements. 
        For instance,  $\Pa{\mathbf{X}}{\mathcal{G}}=\bigcup_{X \in \mathbf{X}}\Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pa, Ch, Anc denote parents, children, ancestors of a vertex, extended to sets by union.

nodes.name: Semi-Markovian assumption
nodes.statement: We assume $\mathcal{G}$ is semi-Markovian, that is for each $U \in \mathbf{U}$, $\Pa{U}{\mathcal{G}}= \varnothing$ and $|\Ch{U}{\mathcal{G}}|=2$.
nodes.statement_short: Every unobserved variable has no parents and exactly two children.

nodes.name: Causal graph of an SEM
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{G}$ is a causal graph for SEM $\mathcal{M}$ if each $X\!\in\! \mathbf{V} \cup \mathbf{U}$ is generated as $f_X(\Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}}, \epsilon_X)$, where $\{\epsilon_X\!: X\in \mathbf{V}\}$ is a set of mutually independent exogenous random variables.
nodes.statement_short: G is the causal graph of SEM M if each variable is a function of its G-parents and independent noise.

nodes.name: Joint distribution of an SEM
nodes.statement: We denote by $P^{\mathcal{M}}(\cdot)$ the joint distribution of the variables in $\mathcal{M}$ and drop the superscript $\mathcal{M}$ when it is clear from the context.

nodes.name: Markov factorization property
nodes.statement: P(\mathbf{v})= \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{X \in \mathbf{V}}P(x|\Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}}P(u),
nodes.statement_short: Observed joint distribution factorizes as a sum over U of products of conditionals given parents.
conclusions:
\label{eq: factorization 1}
            P(\mathbf{v})= \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{X \in \mathbf{V}}P(x|\Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}}P(u),
nodes.label: eq: factorization 1

nodes.name: Positive SEM class M+(G)
nodes.statement:
$\mathbb{M}(\mathcal{G})$ denotes the set of SEMs with causal graph $\mathcal{G}$. 
            $\mathbb{M}^{+}(\mathcal{G})$ denotes the set of SEMs $\mathcal{M} \in \mathbb{M}(\mathcal{G})$  such that $P^{\mathcal{M}}(\mathbf{v})>0$ for each $\mathbf{v} \in \dom{\mathbf{V}}$.
nodes.statement_short: M(G) is the set of SEMs with causal graph G; M+(G) those with strictly positive observational distribution.

nodes.name: Intervention do(X=x)
nodes.statement: For $\mathbf{X} \subseteq \mathbf{V}$ and $\mathbf{x} \in \dom{\mathbf{X}}$, the intervention $do(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$ converts $\mathcal{M}$ to a new SEM where the equations of $\mathbf{X}$ in $\mathcal{M}$ are replaced by the constants in $\mathbf{x}$.

nodes.name: Post-interventional distribution
nodes.statement: We denote by $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\cdot)$ the corresponding post interventional distribution.

nodes.name: Positivity of interventional conditionals
nodes.statement:
For three disjoint subsets $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{W}$ of $\mathbf{V}$, if $\mathcal{M} \in \mathbb{M}^+(\mathcal{G})$, then $P^{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{w})>0$
            for any $\mathbf{x} \in \dom{\mathbf{X}}$, $\mathbf{y} \in \dom{\mathbf{Y}}$, and $\mathbf{w} \in \dom{\mathbf{W}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Under positivity, every post-interventional conditional probability is strictly positive.

nodes.name: Q[S] interventional distribution
nodes.statement_short: Q[S](v) is the distribution of S under intervention on all other observed variables.

nodes.name: Definition of Q[S]
nodes.statement: Q[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}) := P_{\mathbf{v}\setminus \mathbf{s}}(\mathbf{s}).
nodes.label: eq: Q

nodes.name: Factorization of Q[S]
nodes.statement: Q[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v})= \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{S \in \mathbf{S}}P(s|\Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}}P(u).
nodes.statement_short: Q[S] factorizes as a sum over U of products of conditionals of S given parents.
nodes.label: eq: factorization 2

nodes.name: Induced subgraph G[X]
nodes.statement: For $\mathbf{X} \subseteq \mathbf{V}$, $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{X}]$ denotes the inducing subgraph of $\mathcal{G}$ over $\mathbf{X}$ and the unobserved variables with both children in $\mathbf{X}$.

nodes.name: Projected graph G_X
nodes.statement: Furthermore, we denote by $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}}$ the partially directed graph over $\mathbf{X}$ obtained by removing unobserved variables of $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{X}]$ and replacing them by bidirected edges.

nodes.name: c-component and c-forest
nodes.statement:
For $\mathbf{X} \subseteq \mathbf{V}$, confounded components or c-components of $\mathbf{X}$ are the connected components of the graph obtained by only the bidirected edges of $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}}$.
            Also, a subgraph of $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V}}$ is called a single c-component if its bidirected edges form a connected graph. 
            Suppose $\mathcal{H}$ is a subgraph of $\mathcal{G}$ over observed vertices $\mathbf{X}$. 
            The root set of $\mathcal{H}$ is the maximal subset of $\mathbf{X}$ with no children in $\mathcal{H}$. 
            $\mathcal{H}$ is called $\mathbf{R}$-rooted c-forest if $\mathbf{R}$ is the root set of $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}}$ is a single c-component, and each node in $\mathbf{X}$ has at most one child in $\mathcal{H}$.
nodes.statement_short: c-components are connected components of bidirected edges; an R-rooted c-forest is a single c-component with root set R and at most one child per node.
nodes.label: def: c-component and c-forest

nodes.name: Example 1
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Example 1:}
        Consider the causal graph $\mathcal{G}$ in Figure \ref{fig: G}, where $\mathbf{V} = \{X_1,X_2,Y_1,Y_2\}$ and $\mathbf{U} = \{U_1,U_2\}$.
        $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V}}$ is depicted in Figure \ref{fig: Gv}.
        The c-components of $\mathbf{V}$ are $\{X_1,X_2\}$ and $\{Y_1,Y_2\}$.
        Figure \ref{fig: G[X1,X2]} depicts the inducing subgraph of $\mathcal{G}$ over $\{X_1,X_2\}$ and $\mathcal{G}_{\{X_1,X_2\}}$ is depicted in Figure \ref{fig: G_X1,X2}. 
        Herein, $\mathcal{G}[\{X_1,X_2\}]$ is $\{X_1,X_2\}$-rooted c-forest since $\mathcal{G}_{\{X_1,X_2\}}$ is single c-component.
nodes.statement_short: A four-variable graph illustrating G_V, c-components, induced subgraphs and a c-forest.

nodes.name: Identifiability
nodes.statement:
Suppose $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are two disjoint subsets of $\mathbf{V}$.
            The causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is said to be identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$ if for any $\mathbf{x} \in \dom{\mathbf{X}}$ and $\mathbf{y} \in \dom{\mathbf{Y}}$, $P^{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is uniquely computable from $P^{\mathcal{M}}(\mathbf{V})$ in any SEM $\mathcal{M} \in \mathbb{M}^{+}(\mathcal{G})$.
            Also, $Q[\mathbf{Y}]$ is said to be identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$ if the causal effect of $\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{Y}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: A causal effect is identifiable if it is uniquely computable from P(V) in every positive SEM with graph G.
nodes.label: def: id

nodes.name: Reduction of causal effect identifiability to Q[Anc]
nodes.statement: The causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$ if and only $Q[\Anc{\mathbf{Y}}{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}}}]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$.
conclusions:
\label{prp: 1}
            The causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$ if and only $Q[\Anc{\mathbf{Y}}{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}}}]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$.
equivalent_conditions: The causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$
nodes.statement_short: P_x(y) is identifiable iff Q of the ancestors of Y in G_{V\X} is identifiable.
nodes.label: prp: 1

nodes.name: c-component decomposition of identifiability
nodes.statement: Suppose $\mathbf{S}_1,\cdots,\mathbf{S}_l$ are the c-components of $\mathbf{S}\subseteq \mathbf{V}$. $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$ if and only if $Q[\mathbf{S}_i]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$ for all $i\in [1:l]$.
conclusions: $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$ if and only if $Q[\mathbf{S}_i]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$ for all $i\in [1:l]$
nodes.statement_short: Q[S] is identifiable iff Q of each c-component of S is identifiable.
nodes.label: prp: 2

nodes.name: ID algorithm (Tian-Pearl identifiability)
nodes.statement:
\caption{Identifiability} \begin{algorithmic}[1]
                \STATE \textbf{Function ID}($\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathcal{G}$)
                \STATE \textbf{Output:} True, if the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$. 
                \STATE $\mathbf{S} \gets \Anc{\mathbf{Y}}{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}}}$
                \STATE $\{\mathbf{S}_1,\dots,\mathbf{S}_l\} \gets$ c-components of $\mathbf{S}$
                \FOR{$i$ from $1$ to $l$}
                    \IF{\textbf{ID\_Single}($\mathbf{S}_i,\mathcal{G}$) = False}
                        \STATE \textbf{Return} False
                    \ENDIF
                \ENDFOR
                \STATE \textbf{Return} True
            \end{algorithmic}
            \hrulefill
            \begin{algorithmic}[1]
                \STATE \textbf{Function ID\_Single}($\mathbf{S},\mathcal{G}$)
                \STATE \textbf{Output:} True, if $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$, where $\mathbf{S}$ is a single c-component.
                \STATE $\mathbf{Y} \gets \mathbf{V}$
                \WHILE{$\mathbf{Y} \neq \mathbf{S}$}
                    \STATE $\mathbf{A} \gets \Anc{\mathbf{S}}{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{Y}}}$
                    \STATE $\mathbf{Y}_{new} \gets $ The c-component of $\mathbf{A}$ that contains $\mathbf{S}$
                    \IF{$\mathbf{Y}_{new} = \mathbf{Y}$}
                        \STATE \textbf{Return} False
                    \ELSE
                        \STATE $\mathbf{Y} \gets \mathbf{Y}_{new}$
                    \ENDIF
                \ENDWHILE
                \STATE \textbf{Return} True
            \end{algorithmic}
output: True, if the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: Decides identifiability: reduce to ancestors, split into c-components, and shrink each via ID_Single ancestral/c-component iterations.
nodes.label: algo: ID

nodes.name: Soundness and completeness of the ID algorithm
nodes.statement: This algorithm is both sound and complete \citep{shpitser2006identification, huang2008completeness}.
conclusions: This algorithm is both sound and complete

nodes.name: g-identifiability (Lee et al.)
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}$ be disjoint subsets of $\mathbf{V}$, $\mathbb{Z}=\{\mathbf{Z}_i\}_{i=0}^{m}$ be a collection of subsets of $\mathbf{V}$, and let $\mathcal{G}$ be a causal diagram. 
            $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is said to be g-identifiable from $\mathbb{Z}$ in $\mathcal{G}$, if $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is uniquely computable from distributions $\{P(\mathbf{V}|do(\mathbf{z}))\}_{\mathbf{Z}\in \mathbb{Z}, \mathbf{z}\in \dom{\mathbf{Z}}}$ in any causal model which induces $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: P_x(y) is g-identifiable from Z if computable from the do(z) distributions in any causal model inducing G (no positivity).
nodes.label: def: gid_old

nodes.name: g-identifiability (with positivity)
nodes.statement:
Suppose $\mathbb{A}=\{\mathbf{A}_i\}_{i=0}^m$ is a collection of subsets of $\mathbf{V}$ and $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}$ are two disjoint subsets of $\mathbf{V}$.
            The causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is said to be g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$ if for any $\mathbf{x} \in \dom{\mathbf{X}}$ and $\mathbf{y} \in \dom{\mathbf{Y}}$, $P^{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is uniquely computable from the set of distributions $\{Q[\mathbf{A}_i]\}_{i=0}^m$ in any SEM $\mathcal{M} \in \mathbb{M}^{+}(\mathcal{G})$.
            Also, $Q[\mathbf{Y}]$ is said to be g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$ if the causal effect of $\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{Y}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
nodes.statement_short: A causal effect is g-identifiable from (A,G) if uniquely computable from {Q[A_i]} in every positive SEM with graph G.
nodes.label: def: gid

nodes.name: Equivalence of the two gID definitions up to positivity
nodes.statement: Note that knowing $P(\mathbf{V}|do(\mathbf{Z}))$ for some subset $\mathbf{Z}\subseteq\mathbf{V}$ is equivalent to knowing $Q[\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{Z}]$, and therefore, by setting $\mathbf{A}_i = \mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{Z}_i$, the two aforementioned definitions are the same except for the positivity assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Setting A_i = V\Z_i makes the old and new gID definitions coincide except for positivity.

nodes.name: Do-calculus unsound without positivity
nodes.statement: The following example shows that do-calculus-based methods (e.g., Algorithm \ref{algo: ID}) are no longer sound for the ID problem ignoring the positivity assumption.
conclusions: do-calculus-based methods (e.g., Algorithm \ref{algo: ID}) are no longer sound for the ID problem ignoring the positivity assumption

nodes.name: Example 2
nodes.statement_short: Two non-positive binary SEMs on the Fig. 1 graph agree observationally but differ under intervention, so do-calculus and Lee et al.'s algorithm are unsound.

nodes.name: Completeness proof of Lee et al. relies on non-positive models
nodes.statement:
\citep{lee2019general} presented necessary and sufficient conditions to determine if a causal effect $P_{\textbf{x}}(\textbf{y})$ is g-identifiable w.r.t. the Definition \ref{def: gid_old}.
        To prove that their proposed conditions are necessary for g-identifiability, they construct two models $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$ such that the available distributions in the definition of the problem are the same for both models yet $P^{\mathcal{M}_1}_{\textbf{x}}(\textbf{y})\neq P^{\mathcal{M}_2}_{\textbf{x}}(\textbf{y})$.
        The issue here is that they constructed their models ignoring the positivity assumption, allowing for zero probability for some realizations. 
        In fact, having zero probabilities in their model is essential for the proof. 
        For instance, Lemma 3 in \cite{lee2019general} states that under certain conditions, there is an observed variable $R\in \mathbf{V}$ such that it takes value zero in both their models with probability one.
        In other words, the probability of $R$ not being zero is zero (see Appendix \ref{apn: pos assumption simple} for more details.)
        This shows that adding the positivity assumption to the definition of gID will fail the proof technique in \citep{lee2019general} for the completeness of their proposed algorithm.
nodes.statement_short: Lee et al.'s completeness proof builds models with zero-probability events, so it fails under positivity.

nodes.name: Soundness of do-calculus under relaxed positivity
nodes.statement:
\cite{shpitser2006identification} show that in the ID problem of a causal effect \mbox{$P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$}, one can relax the positivity constraint \mbox{$P(\mathbf{V})>0$} to \mbox{$P(\mathbf{X}|\left(\Pa{\mathbf{X}}{\mathcal{G}}\cap\mathbf{V}\right) \setminus \mathbf{X})>0$}.
        They show that the rules of do-calculus are sound under the relaxed positivity assumption.
conclusions: the rules of do-calculus are sound under the relaxed positivity assumption
nodes.statement_short: Positivity can be relaxed to P(X | observed parents of X outside X) > 0, under which do-calculus stays sound.

nodes.name: Lee et al. models violate relaxed positivity
nodes.statement:
More precisely, consider the causal graph $\mathcal{G}$ in \mbox{Figure \ref{fig:countr_exmpl_complex}} which is brought here from \cite{lee2019general}. 
        Assume that we are interested in g-identifying the causal effect $Q[R]$ from $\mathbb{Z}=\{\varnothing\}$, i.e., from mere observational distribution $P(\mathbf{V})$, w.r.t. Definition \ref{def: gid_old}.
        In this case, $\mathbf{X}=\{T_1, T_2, T_3\}$ and therefore:
        \begin{equation*}
            P(\mathbf{X}|\left(\Pa{\mathbf{X}}{\mathcal{G}}\cap\mathbf{V}\right) \setminus \mathbf{X}) = P(T_1, T_2, T_3).  
        \end{equation*}
        
        The result in \cite{lee2019general} implies that the causal effect $Q[R]$ is not g-identifiable given the causal graph $\mathcal{G}$ in Figure \ref{fig:countr_exmpl_complex}. 
        To prove the non g-identifiability, \cite{lee2019general} constructed two models $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$ that impose similar observational distributions, i.e., $P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(\mathbf{V})=P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(\mathbf{V})$, while the causal effect $Q[R]$ under these two models are not the same for at least one realization. 
        Next, we present these two models and show that they violate the positivity assumption claimed in \cite{shpitser2006identification}, i.e., $P(T_1,T_2,T_3)$ is zero for certain realizations of $\{T_1,T_2,T_3\}$.
        
        By the construction in \cite{lee2019general}, variables $T_3, U_1, U_2, U_3$ are binary variables and $T_1, T_2$ are binary vectors of length two. 
        For both models, all unobserved variables are defined to be binary with uniform distribution, and the observed variables $T_1, T_2, T_3$ are defined as follows.
        \begin{align*}
            &T_3 = U_2 \oplus U_3,\\
            &T_{2, 1} = T_3,\quad  T_{2, 2} = U_1,\\
            &T_{1, 1} = T_{2, 1}\oplus U_2,\quad T_{1, 2} = T_{2, 2}.  
        \end{align*}
        In model $\mathcal{M}_1$, variable $R$ is defined as
        \begin{equation*}
            R = \mathds{1}_{T_{1, 1} = 0} \wedge \mathds{1}_{T_{1, 2}=0} \wedge \mathds{1}_{U_3=1} \wedge \mathds{1}_{U_{1} = 1},
        \end{equation*}
        and in model $\mathcal{M}_2$, it is defined to be zero, i.e., $R = 0.$
        
        Given the above models, it is clear that the probability $P(t_1, t_2, t_3)$ is equal to zero whenever $t_{2,1}\neq t_3$, and therefore, the relaxed positivity constraint \mbox{$P(T_1, T_2, T_3)>0$} does not hold for the models in \cite{lee2019general}.
nodes.statement_short: The two models Lee et al. use for the Fig. 2 graph give P(t1,t2,t3)=0 when t_{2,1} differs from t3.

nodes.name: Reduction of g-identifiability to Q[Anc]
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ be two disjoint subsets of $\mathbf{V}$.
        The causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$ if and only if $Q[\Anc{\mathbf{Y}}{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}}}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$.
assumptions: $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ be two disjoint subsets of $\mathbf{V}$
conclusions: The causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$ if and only if $Q[\Anc{\mathbf{Y}}{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}}}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$
equivalent_conditions: The causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$
nodes.statement_short: g-identifiability of P_x(y) is equivalent to that of Q on the ancestors of Y in G_{V\X}.
also_stated_at:
Let $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ be two disjoint subsets of $\mathbf{V}$.
            The causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$ if and only if $Q[\Anc{\mathbf{Y}}{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}}}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$.
nodes.label: prp: 3

nodes.name: c-component decomposition of g-identifiability
nodes.statement:
Suppose $\mathbf{S}_1,\cdots,\mathbf{S}_l$ are the c-components of $\mathbf{S} \subseteq \mathbf{V}$. 
        $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$ if and only if $Q[\mathbf{S}_i]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$ for all $i\in [1:l]$.
conclusions: $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$ if and only if $Q[\mathbf{S}_i]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$ for all $i\in [1:l]$
nodes.statement_short: Q[S] is g-identifiable iff each of its c-components is.
also_stated_at:
Suppose $\mathbf{S}\subseteq \mathbf{V}$ and $\mathbf{S}_1,\cdots,\mathbf{S}_l$ are the c-components of $\mathbf{S}$. 
            $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$ if and only if $Q[\mathbf{S}_i]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$ for each $i\in [1:l]$.
nodes.label: prp: 4

nodes.name: gID reduces to classical ID (Theorem 1)
nodes.statement:
Suppose $\mathbf{S} \subseteq \mathbf{V}$ is a single c-component. 
        $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$ if and only if there exists $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{A}$ such that $\mathbf{S} \subseteq \mathbf{A}$ and $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]$.
conclusions: $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$ if and only if there exists $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{A}$ such that $\mathbf{S} \subseteq \mathbf{A}$ and $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]$
equivalent_conditions: there exists $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{A}$ such that $\mathbf{S} \subseteq \mathbf{A}$ and $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]$
nodes.statement_short: For a single c-component S, Q[S] is g-identifiable iff Q[S] is identifiable from G[A] for some available A containing S.
nodes.label: thm: main

nodes.name: GID algorithm
nodes.statement:
\caption{g-identifiability} \begin{algorithmic}[1]
            \STATE \textbf{Function GID}($\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbb{A}=\{\mathbf{A}_i\}_{i=0}^m ,\mathcal{G}$)
            \STATE \textbf{Output:} True, if the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$. 
            \STATE $\mathbf{S} \gets \Anc{\mathbf{Y}}{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}}}$
            \STATE $\{\mathbf{S}_1,\dots,\mathbf{S}_l\} \gets$ c-components of $\mathbf{S}$
            \FOR{$i$ from $1$ to $l$}
                \IF{\textbf{GID\_Single}($\mathbf{S}_i,\mathbb{A}=\{\mathbf{A}_i\}_{i=0}^m ,\mathcal{G}$) = False}
                    \STATE \textbf{Return} False
                \ENDIF
            \ENDFOR
            \STATE \textbf{Return} True
        \end{algorithmic}
        \hrulefill
        \begin{algorithmic}[1]
            \STATE \textbf{Function GID\_Single}($\mathbf{S}, \mathbb{A}=\{\mathbf{A}_i\}_{i=0}^m, \mathcal{G}$)
            \STATE \textbf{Output:} True, if $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$, where $\mathbf{S}$ is a single c-component.
            \FOR{$i$ from $0$ to $m$}
                \IF{$\mathbf{S} \subseteq \mathbf{A}_i$ and \textbf{ID\_Single}($\mathbf{S}, \mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}_i]$) = True}
                    \STATE \textbf{Return} True
                \ENDIF
            \ENDFOR
            \STATE \textbf{Return} False
        \end{algorithmic}
output: True, if the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$.
nodes.statement_short: Decides g-identifiability: split ancestors of Y into c-components and check each with ID_Single in G[A_i] for some A_i containing it.
nodes.label: algo: GID

nodes.name: Soundness and completeness of GID
nodes.statement: Algorithm \ref{algo: GID} is sound and complete.
conclusions: Algorithm \ref{algo: GID} is sound and complete.

nodes.name: Proof of soundness and completeness of GID
nodes.statement: It directly follows from Propositions \ref{prp: 3} and \ref{prp: 4} and Theorem \ref{thm: main}.
nodes.statement_short: Direct combination of Propositions 3, 4 and Theorem 1.

nodes.name: GID under relaxed positivity
nodes.statement: Under the relaxed positivity assumption, the algorithm is still sound and complete because Algorithm \ref{algo: GID} is based on the rules of do-calculus, and these rules are both sound and complete under the relaxed positivity assumption.
nodes.statement_short: GID remains sound and complete under relaxed positivity since it rests on do-calculus.

nodes.name: Formula derivation for a g-identifiable causal effect
nodes.statement_short: Derive P_x(Y): get Q[S_i] via ID_Single, multiply over c-components, then marginalize S\Y.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
In this section, we present the main steps of the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: main}.
    The technical lemmas in this section are proved in Appendix \ref{sec: apd_proof}. 

    \paragraph{Sufficient part:}
    This part is straightforward: if $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]$ for some $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{A}$ such that $\mathbf{S} \subseteq \mathbf{A}$, then $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is uniquely computable from $Q[\mathbf{A}]$, and therefore, $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$.
    
    \paragraph{Necessary part:}
    Suppose $\mathbf{S}$ is a single c-component and  $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not identifiable from $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}_i]$ for all $\mathbf{A}_i \in \mathbb{A}$ such that $\mathbf{S} \subseteq \mathbf{A}_i$. 
    We need to show that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$.
    Recall that $\mathbb{A}=\{\mathbf{A}_i\}_{i=0}^m$.
    To this end, we will introduce two SEMs $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$ in $\mathbb{M^+(\mathcal{G})}$ such that for each $i\in [0:m]$ and any $\mathbf{v} \in \dom{\mathbf{V}}$,
    \begin{equation} Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}), 
    \end{equation}
    but there exists $\mathbf{v}_0 \in \dom{\mathbf{V}}$ such that 
    \begin{equation} Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}_0) \neq Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}_0).
    \end{equation}
    This shows that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ cannot be uniquely computed from $\{Q[\mathbf{A}_i]\}_{i=0}^m$.
    
    For sake of space, we assume that there exists at least one $i\in [0, m]$ such that $\mathbf{S}\subset \mathbf{A}_i$. 
    In this case, without loss of generality, we assume that there exists $k \in [0:m]$ such that  $\mathbf{S}\subset \mathbf{A}_i$ for $i\in [0:k]$ and $\mathbf{S}\nsubseteq \mathbf{A}_i$ for $i\in [k+1:m]$.
    A proof for the case in which $\mathbf{S}$ is not a subset of $\mathbf{A}_i$ for all $i\in [0, m]$ is provided in Appendix \ref{sec: apd_second case}.
    
    We first modify $\mathcal{G}$ by deleting some nodes and edges and show that it is enough to prove Theorem \ref{thm: main} for the modified graph. 
    Then, we provide our method for constructing $\mathcal{M}_2$ from $\mathcal{M}_1$ by introducing a system of linear equations.

    \paragraph{Graph modification:} Since $\mathbf{S}$ is single c-component, the bidirected edges in $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{S}}$ form a connected graph over $\mathbf{S}$. 
    Let $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}$ be a minimal (in terms of edges) spanning subgraph of $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{S}]$ such that $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{S}}$ is single c-component. 
    Thus, $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{S}}$ has no directed edges, and its bidirected edges form a spanning tree.
    \begin{lemma}[\cite{shpitser2006identification}] Suppose \mbox{$\mathbf{S} \subseteq\mathbf{A} \subseteq \mathbf{V}$}. 
        $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not identifiable from $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]$ if and only if there exists at least one $\mathbf{S}$-rooted c-forest  $\mathcal{F}$ with the set of observed variables $\mathbf{B}$ such that $\mathbf{S}\subsetneq \mathbf{B} \subseteq \mathbf{A}$, the bidirected edges of $\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{B}}$ form a spanning tree, and the induced subgraph of $\mathcal{F}$ over $\mathbf{S}$ is $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}$, i.e.,  $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}= \mathcal{F}[\mathbf{S}]$.
    \end{lemma}
    Recall that for each $i \in [0:k]$, $\mathbf{S}\subset \mathbf{A}_i$ and $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not identifiable from $Q[\mathbf{A}_i]$. 
    Hence, Lemma \ref{lem: c-forest existence} implies that for each $i\in [0:k]$, there exists a $\mathbf{S}$-rooted c-forest $\mathcal{F}_i$ over a set of observed variables $\mathbf{B}_i$ such that $\mathbf{S}\subsetneq \mathbf{B}_i \subseteq \mathbf{A}_i$, the bidirected edges of $(\mathcal{F}_i)_{\mathbf{S}}$ form a spanning tree, and $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}} = \mathcal{F}_i[\mathbf{S}]$. 
    Next, we use $\{\mathcal{F}_i\}_{i=0}^k$ to modify $\mathcal{G}$.

    We define $\mathcal{G}'$ to be the union of all the subgraphs in $\{\mathcal{F}_i\}_{i=0}^k$ with the observed variables $\mathbf{V}' := \bigcup_{i=0}^k \mathbf{B}_i$ and unobserved variables $\mathbf{U}'$.
    Furthermore, let $\mathbb{A}':= \{\mathbf{A}_i':=\mathbf{A}_i \cap \mathbf{V}'\}_{i=0}^m$. 
    Because for each $i\in [0:k]$, $\mathcal{F}_i$ is a $\mathbf{S}$-rooted c-forest in $\mathcal{G}'$, Lemma \ref{lem: c-forest existence} implies that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not identifiable from $\mathcal{G}'[\mathbf{A}_i']$.

    Next result establishes the connection between non g-identifiability of $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$ and non g-identifiability of $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ from $(\mathbb{A}', \mathcal{G}')$.
    \begin{lemma} If $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}', \mathcal{G}')$, then $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
    \end{lemma}
    To complete the proof using Lemma \ref{lem: simplify}, it is enough to show that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}', \mathcal{G}')$.
    
    \paragraph{From g-identifiability to a system of linear equations:} To show  that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}', \mathcal{G}')$, we introduce two models in $\mathbb{M^+(\mathcal{G}')}$ such that equations \eqref{eq: same Q over A} and \eqref{eq: diff Q over S} are satisfied. 
    That is, $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ cannot be uniquely computed from $\{Q[\mathbf{A}'_i]\}_{i=0}^m$.
    
    Note that to define a SEM $\mathcal{M}$ over a causal graph $\mathcal{G}'$, it suffices to define the domains $\dom{X}$ and either the conditional distributions $P^{\mathcal{M}}(X|\Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}'})$ or the corresponding equation in the SEM for all  $X\in \mathbf{V}'\cup \mathbf{U}'$, where $\mathbf{V}'$ and $\mathbf{U}'$ denote the observed and unobserved variables in $\mathcal{G}'$. 
    We define the domains of all variables to be finite, i.e., $|\dom{X}|<\infty$ for all $X\in\mathbf{V}'\cup \mathbf{U}'$.
    Let $U_0 \in \mathbf{U}'$ be a fixed unobserved variable (we will discuss later how to select $U_0$) with domain $\dom{U_0} := \{\gamma_1,\cdots,\gamma_d\}$.
    We define both models $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$ to have similar distributions over all variables except variable $U_0$ (We will specify these distributions in Section \ref{sec: M1}.)
    More specifically, for all $V \in \mathbf{V}'$,
    \begin{equation} P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(V \mid \Pa{V}{\mathcal{G}'}) = P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(V \mid \Pa{V}{\mathcal{G}'}),
    \end{equation}
    and for all $U \in \mathbf{U}' \setminus \{U_0\}$,
    \begin{equation} P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(U) = P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(U)=\frac{1}{|\dom{U}|}.
    \end{equation}
    As the distributions in Equations \eqref{eq: same dist 1} and \eqref{eq: same dist 2} are the same for both models, for the sake of brevity, we drop the superscripts $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$ from here on.
    For $j\in[1:d]$, We define $P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(U_0=\gamma_j)=1/d$ and $P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(U_0 = \gamma_j)=p_j$, where we will specify $\{p_j\}_{j=1}^d$ later such that $\mathcal{M}_2\in\mathbb{M}^+(\mathcal{G}')$ and both Equations \eqref{eq: same Q over A} and \eqref{eq: diff Q over S} hold.
    
    For $\mathbf{v} \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$, $i\in [0:m]$, and $j\in [1:d]$, we define
    \begin{equation*}
        \theta_{i, j}(\mathbf{v}) :=\! \sum_{\mathbf{U}' \setminus \{U_0\}} \prod_{X \in \mathbf{A}_i'} P(x \mid \Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}'})\! \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}' \setminus \{U_0\}}\! P(u),
    \end{equation*}
    \begin{equation*}
        \eta_j(\mathbf{v}) :=\! \sum_{\mathbf{U}'\setminus \{U_0\}} \prod_{X \in \mathbf{S}} P(x \mid \Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}'})\! \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}'\setminus \{U_0\}}\! P(u),
    \end{equation*}
    where the index $j$ indicates that $U_0=\gamma_j$ in the factorizations. 
    Using these definitions, we can write $\{Q[\mathbf{A}'_i]\}_{i=0}^m$ and $Q[\textbf{S}]$ for both models $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$ as follows:
    \begin{equation} \begin{split}
        Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{A}'_i](\mathbf{v}) 
        = \sum_{j=1}^d \frac{1}{d} \theta_{i,j}(\mathbf{v}), \\
        Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{A}'_i](\mathbf{v}) 
        = \sum_{j=1}^d p_j \theta_{i,j}(\mathbf{v}),
    \end{split}
    \end{equation}
    and
    \begin{equation} \begin{split}
        Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}) 
        &= \sum_{j=1}^d \frac{1}{d} \eta_j(\mathbf{v}), \\
        Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}) 
        &= \sum_{j=1}^d p_j \eta_j(\mathbf{v}).
    \end{split}
    \end{equation}
    As we mentioned, we need to define $\{p_j\}_{j=1}^d$ such that $\mathcal{M}_2 \in \mathbb{M^+(\mathcal{G}')}$ and both Equations \eqref{eq: same Q over A} and \eqref{eq: diff Q over S} hold.
    Substituting Equations \eqref{eq: Q[A] with c} and \eqref{eq: Q[S] with c} into \eqref{eq: same Q over A} and \eqref{eq: diff Q over S} yield the following set of equations.
    \begin{equation} \begin{split}
        &\sum_{j=1}^d (p_j - \frac{1}{d}) \theta_{i,j}(\mathbf{v}) =0, \hspace{0.2cm}\forall \mathbf{v} \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}, i\in [0,m],\\
        &\sum_{j=1}^d (p_j - \frac{1}{d}) \eta_j(\mathbf{v}_0) \neq 0, \hspace{0.2cm} \exists \mathbf{v}_0 \in \dom{\mathbf{V};},\\
        & \sum_{j=1}^d p_j = 1,\\
        & 0<p_j<1, \hspace{0.2cm} \forall j \in [1:d].
    \end{split}
    \end{equation}
    Note that the last inequalities ensure that $\mathcal{M}_2 \in \mathbb{M^+(\mathcal{G}')}$.
    The system of linear equations in \eqref{eq: linear system 1} is solvable with respect to  $\{p_j\}_{j=1}^d$ if and only if the following system of linear equations is solvable with respect to $\{\beta_j\}_{j=1}^d$.
    \begin{equation} \begin{split}
        &\sum_{j=1}^d \beta_j \theta_{i,j}(\mathbf{v}) =0, \hspace{0.2cm}\forall \mathbf{v} \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}, i \in [0:m]\\
        &\sum_{j=1}^d \beta_j \eta_j(\mathbf{v}_0) \neq 0, \hspace{0.2cm} \exists \mathbf{v}_0 \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}\\
        & \sum_{j=1}^d \beta_j=0.
    \end{split}
    \end{equation}
    
    \begin{remark}
        If $\{\beta_j^*\}_{j=1}^d$ is a solution for \eqref{eq: linear system 2}, then
        \begin{equation} p_j^* := \frac{1}{d} + \frac{\beta^*_j}{2h d},
        \end{equation}
        is a solution for \eqref{eq: linear system 1}, where $h = \underset{j \in [1:d]}{max} |\beta^*_j|$. 
        Note that the division by $2h$ in Equation \eqref{eq: system to system} ensures that $0< p_j^* <1$ for each $j \in [1:d]$.
    \end{remark}
    A solution to the system of linear equations in \eqref{eq: linear system 2} will specify the distribution of $U_0$ in model $\mathcal{M}_2$. Clearly, existence of a solution to \eqref{eq: linear system 2} depends on the choices of $\{\theta_{i,j}(\mathbf{v})\}$ and $\{\eta_j(\mathbf{v})\}$. 
    The following result presents a sufficient condition under which \eqref{eq: linear system 2} admits a solution.
    
    For $\mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$ and $i\in [0:m]$, let $\theta_i(\mathbf{v})$ and $\eta(\mathbf{v})$ denote the vectors $(\theta_{i,1}(\mathbf{v}),...,\theta_{i,d}(\mathbf{v}))$  and $(\eta_1(\mathbf{v}),...,\eta_d(\mathbf{v}))$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, respectively.
    \begin{lemma} Consider the following set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$
         \begin{equation} \mathbf{\Omega}:=\{\theta_{i}(\mathbf{v}):\ i\in [0:m], \mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}\} \cup \{\mathds{1}_d\},
        \end{equation}
        where $\mathds{1}_d$ denotes the all-ones vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$. 
        If there exists $\mathbf{v}_0 \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$ such that $\eta(\mathbf{v}_0)$ is linearly independent from all the vectors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$, then the system of linear equations in \eqref{eq: linear system 2} admits a solution. 
    \end{lemma}
    To summarize, so far, we have introduced two models for proving the necessary part of Theorem \ref{thm: main}. 
    In order to complete the proof, it remains to specify the conditional distributions in \eqref{eq: same dist 1} for all observed variables which consequently specify the vectors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$ in Equation \eqref{eq: lin vectors} and to find a realization $\mathbf{v}_0 \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$ such that $\eta(\mathbf{v}_0)$ is linearly independent from the set of the vectors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$.
    
    
    \paragraph{Constructing the conditional distributions:} In order to specify the conditional distributions in \eqref{eq: same dist 1}, we first introduce the following definitions and notations. 
    
    Since $\mathbf{B}_0$ is a single c-component, the bidirected edges in $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{B}_0}'$ form a connected graph.
    Hence, there exists a bidirected edge between $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{B}_0 \setminus \mathbf{S}$.
    Accordingly, let $U_0$ be an unobserved variable in subgraph $\mathcal{F}_0$ that has one child in $\mathbf{S}$ and one child in $\mathbf{T} := \mathbf{V}' \setminus \mathbf{S}$.
    We denote the set of unobserved variables in $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{S}]$ by $\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}$ and define  $\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{T}} := \mathbf{U}' \setminus ( \mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}} \cup \{U_0\})$. 
    For $X \in \mathbf{V}' \cup \mathbf{U}'$, we define $\alpha(X)$ to denote the number of graphs in $\{\mathcal{F}_j\}_{j=0}^{k}$ that contains $X$.
    
    For each $i\in [0:k]$, let $T_i$ denotes a node in $\mathbf{B}_i \setminus \mathbf{S}$ such that $\Ch{T_i}{\mathcal{F}_i} \cap \mathbf{S} \neq \varnothing$. 
    Note that such variables exist because $\mathcal{F}_i$s are $\mathbf{S}$-rooted c-forest. 

    Now, we are ready to introduce the domains of all variables in $\mathbf{V}'\cup\mathbf{U}'$. Recall that $\mathbf{V}'=\textbf{S}\cup\mathbf{T}$ and $\mathbf{U}'=\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}} \cup \mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{T}} \cup \{U_0\}$.
    \begin{align*}
        &\dom{X} := [0:\kappa], \quad \forall X \in \mathbf{S},\\
        &\dom{X} := \{0, 1\}^{\alpha(T)}, \quad \forall X \in \mathbf{T},\\
        &\dom{X} := [0:\kappa], \quad \forall X \in \mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}},\\
        &\dom{X} := \{0, 1\}^{\alpha(U)}, \quad \forall X \in \mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{T}},\\
        &\dom{U_0} := [0:\kappa]\times\{0, 1\}^{\alpha(U_0)-1}.
    \end{align*}
    In the above definition, $\kappa$ is an arbitrary odd integer greater than $4$. 
    Note that the number of elements in $\dom{U_0}$ is $d=(\kappa+1)2^{\alpha(U_0)-1}$.

    According to the above definitions, for each $X\in \mathbf{T}\cup\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{T}}\cup \{U_0\}$, its domain $\dom{X}$ is a subset of  $\mathbb{R}^{\alpha(X)}$ and it belongs to exactly $\alpha(X)$ number of subgraphs in $\{\mathcal{F}_i\}_{i=0}^k$.
    Suppose $X$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}_{i_1},\cdots, \mathcal{F}_{i_{\alpha(X)}}$, where $i_1 < \cdots < i_{\alpha(X)}$.
    Thus, we denote $X$ by a vector $ (X[i_1],\cdots,X[i_{\alpha(X)}])$ of length $\alpha(X)$. Next, we construct the conditional distributions of the observed variables by specifying their functional dependencies to their parents.
        
    When $X\in \mathbf{T}$, we define the entries of its corresponding vector as
    \begin{equation*}
        X[i_j] \equiv \left(\sum_{Y \in \Pa{X}{\mathcal{F}_{i_j}}} Y[i_j]\right) \pmod{2},
    \end{equation*}
    where $j\in[1:\alpha(X)]$.
    
    We now construct the variables in $\mathbf{S}$. 
    Recall that $U_0$ has one child in $\mathbf{S}$ which we denote it by $S_0$.
    For each $S \in \mathbf{S}\setminus \{S_0\}$ and any realization of $\Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'}$, we define $\mathds{I}(S)$ to be one if there exists $i\in [0:k]$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $T_i \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'}$ and $T_i[i]=0$, or
        \item there exists $X \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'} \setminus (\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}\cup \{T_i\})$ such that $\mathcal{F}_i$ contains $X$ and $X[i]=1$,
    \end{enumerate}
    and zero, otherwise.
    Note that according to the definition of $T_i$, it belongs to $\mathcal{F}_i$ and therefore, $T_i[i]$ exists. 
    Analogously, we define $\mathds{I}(S_0)$ to be one if there exists $i\in [0:k]$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $T_i \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'}$ and $T_i[i]=0$, or
        \item $i\neq0$, $\mathcal{F}_i$ contains $U_0$, and $U_0[i]=1$, or
        \item there exists $X \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'} \setminus (\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}\cup \{T_i,U_0\})$ such that $\mathcal{F}_i$ contains $X$ and $X[i]=1$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    Now, for each $S\in \mathbf{S}$ and $s \in [0:\kappa]$, we define $P(S=s \mid \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'})$ as
    \begin{equation*}
    \begin{cases} 
        \frac{1}{\kappa+1} & \text{ if } \mathds{I}(S)=1\\
        1-\kappa\epsilon &  \text{ if } \mathds{I}(S)=0  \text{ and } s \equiv M(S) \pmod{\kappa+1}, \\
        \epsilon &  \text{ if }  \mathds{I}(S)=0  \text{ and } s\not\equiv M(S) \pmod{\kappa+1},
    \end{cases}
    \end{equation*}
    where $0<\epsilon<\frac{1}{\kappa}$ and 
    \begin{equation*}
    M(S):=
    \begin{cases} 
        \sum_{x\in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'[\mathbf{S}]}}x & \text{, if } S\in \mathbf{S}\setminus \{S_0\}, \\
        u_0[0]+\sum_{x\in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'[\mathbf{S}]}}x & \text{, if $S=S_0$ }.
    \end{cases}
    \end{equation*}
    Note that $M(S)$ is an integer number. This is because $\Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'[\mathbf{S}]}\subseteq \mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}$ and thus all terms in the above definition belong to $[0:\kappa]$. 
    \begin{lemma} The SEM constructed above belongs to $\mathbb{M}^+(\mathcal{G}')$. 
    \end{lemma}


    \paragraph{Existence of realization $\textbf{v}_0$:} Herein, we show that for the aforementioned conditional distributions, there exists a realization $\textbf{v}_0$ such that $\eta(\mathbf{v}_0)$ is linearly independent from the set of the vectors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$ (in Equation \eqref{eq: lin vectors}).  
    Consider the following subset of $\dom{U_0}=\{\gamma_1,...,\gamma_d\}$ with $\frac{\kappa+1}{2}$ elements:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathbf{\Gamma} := \Big\{(2x,0,\cdots,0)\!:\: x\in [0:\frac{\kappa-1}{2}]\Big\}.
    \end{equation*}
    Recall that for $\mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$ and $i\in[0:m]$, $\theta_i(\mathbf{v})$ and $\eta(\mathbf{v})$ are two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $j$-th entry corresponds to $U_0=\gamma_j$. 
    Suppose that $\mathbf{\Gamma}=\{\gamma_{j_1},...,\gamma_{j_{\frac{\kappa+1}{2}}}\}$. Next result shows that in our constructed models, all entries of $\theta_i(\textbf{v})$ with indices in $\{j_1,...,j_{\frac{\kappa+1}{2}}\}$ are equal.
    \begin{lemma} For any $\mathbf{v} \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$ and $i\in[0:m]$,
        \begin{equation*}
            \theta_{i,j_1}(\mathbf{v}) = \theta_{i,j_2}(\mathbf{v}) = \cdots= \theta_{i,j_{\frac{\kappa+1}{2}}}(\mathbf{v}).
        \end{equation*}
    \end{lemma}
    An immediate consequence of this result is that any linear combination of the vectors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$ will have equal entries at the indices in $\{j_1,...,j_{\frac{\kappa+1}{2}}\}$.
    Next, we show there exists a realization $\textbf{v}_0$ for which $\eta(\mathbf{v}_0)$ does not follow this pattern and thus it is linearly independent of all vectors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$.
    \begin{lemma} There exists $0<\epsilon<\frac{1}{\kappa}$ for which there exists $\mathbf{v}_0 \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$ and $1\leq r <t\leq \frac{\kappa+1}{2}$ such that 
        \begin{equation*}
            \eta_{j_r}(\mathbf{v}_0) \neq \eta_{j_t}(\mathbf{v}_0). 
        \end{equation*}
    \end{lemma}
    Lemma \ref{lem: eta index} implies that there exist $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\epsilon$ for which there exists $\mathbf{v}_0 \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$ such that $\eta(\mathbf{v}_0)$ is linearly independent from the set of vectors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$.
    As we discussed before, this completes our proof for Theorem \ref{thm: main}.
nodes.statement_short: Sufficiency is direct; for necessity, reduce G to a union of S-rooted c-forests and build two positive SEMs differing only in U_0's law via a linear system. Key step: entries of theta are equal on Gamma while eta's are not.

nodes.name: c-forest characterization of non-identifiability
nodes.statement:
Suppose \mbox{$\mathbf{S} \subseteq\mathbf{A} \subseteq \mathbf{V}$}. 
        $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not identifiable from $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]$ if and only if there exists at least one $\mathbf{S}$-rooted c-forest  $\mathcal{F}$ with the set of observed variables $\mathbf{B}$ such that $\mathbf{S}\subsetneq \mathbf{B} \subseteq \mathbf{A}$, the bidirected edges of $\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{B}}$ form a spanning tree, and the induced subgraph of $\mathcal{F}$ over $\mathbf{S}$ is $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}$, i.e.,  $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}= \mathcal{F}[\mathbf{S}]$.
conclusions: $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not identifiable from $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]$ if and only if there exists at least one $\mathbf{S}$-rooted c-forest  $\mathcal{F}$ with the set of observed variables $\mathbf{B}$ such that $\mathbf{S}\subsetneq \mathbf{B} \subseteq \mathbf{A}$, the bidirected edges of $\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{B}}$ form a spanning tree, and the induced subgraph of $\mathcal{F}$ over $\mathbf{S}$ is $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}$, i.e.,  $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}= \mathcal{F}[\mathbf{S}]$.
equivalent_conditions: there exists at least one $\mathbf{S}$-rooted c-forest  $\mathcal{F}$ with the set of observed variables $\mathbf{B}$ such that $\mathbf{S}\subsetneq \mathbf{B} \subseteq \mathbf{A}$, the bidirected edges of $\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{B}}$ form a spanning tree, and the induced subgraph of $\mathcal{F}$ over $\mathbf{S}$ is $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}$
nodes.statement_short: Q[S] is not identifiable from G[A] iff an S-rooted c-forest with spanning-tree bidirected edges exists inside A.
nodes.label: lem: c-forest existence

nodes.name: Equal Q over available sets
nodes.statement: Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}),
nodes.label: eq: same Q over A

nodes.name: Different Q over S
nodes.statement: Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}_0) \neq Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}_0).
nodes.label: eq: diff Q over S

nodes.name: Graph simplification preserves non-g-identifiability
nodes.statement: If $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}', \mathcal{G}')$, then $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
conclusions: $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$
nodes.statement_short: Non-g-identifiability in the reduced graph G' transfers to the original graph.
also_stated_at: If $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}', \mathcal{G}')$, then $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
nodes.label: lem: simplify

nodes.name: Same conditionals for observed variables
nodes.statement: P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(V \mid \Pa{V}{\mathcal{G}'}) = P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(V \mid \Pa{V}{\mathcal{G}'}),
nodes.label: eq: same dist 1

nodes.name: Same uniform distribution for unobserved variables except U_0
nodes.statement: P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(U) = P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(U)=\frac{1}{|\dom{U}|}.
nodes.label: eq: same dist 2

nodes.name: Q[A_i'] in terms of theta
nodes.label: eq: Q[A] with c

nodes.name: Q[S] in terms of eta

nodes.name: Linear system for p_j
nodes.statement_short: Linear constraints on U_0's distribution so the two models agree on Q[A_i'] but differ on Q[S].
nodes.label: eq: linear system 1

nodes.name: Homogeneous linear system for beta_j
nodes.label: eq: linear system 2

nodes.name: From beta-solution to p-solution
nodes.statement:
If $\{\beta_j^*\}_{j=1}^d$ is a solution for \eqref{eq: linear system 2}, then
        \begin{equation} p_j^* := \frac{1}{d} + \frac{\beta^*_j}{2h d},
        \end{equation}
        is a solution for \eqref{eq: linear system 1}, where $h = \underset{j \in [1:d]}{max} |\beta^*_j|$. 
        Note that the division by $2h$ in Equation \eqref{eq: system to system} ensures that $0< p_j^* <1$ for each $j \in [1:d]$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescaling a beta solution by 1/(2hd) around the uniform law yields a valid positive p solution.

nodes.name: Definition of p_j*
nodes.statement: p_j^* := \frac{1}{d} + \frac{\beta^*_j}{2h d},
nodes.label: eq: system to system

nodes.name: Linear independence gives a solution
nodes.statement:
Consider the following set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$
         \begin{equation} \mathbf{\Omega}:=\{\theta_{i}(\mathbf{v}):\ i\in [0:m], \mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}\} \cup \{\mathds{1}_d\},
        \end{equation}
        where $\mathds{1}_d$ denotes the all-ones vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$. 
        If there exists $\mathbf{v}_0 \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$ such that $\eta(\mathbf{v}_0)$ is linearly independent from all the vectors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$, then the system of linear equations in \eqref{eq: linear system 2} admits a solution.
assumptions: there exists $\mathbf{v}_0 \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$ such that $\eta(\mathbf{v}_0)$ is linearly independent from all the vectors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$
conclusions: the system of linear equations in \eqref{eq: linear system 2} admits a solution
nodes.statement_short: If eta(v_0) is linearly independent of all theta_i(v) and the all-ones vector, the beta system is solvable.
nodes.label: lem: lin indep

nodes.name: Vector set Omega
nodes.statement: \mathbf{\Omega}:=\{\theta_{i}(\mathbf{v}):\ i\in [0:m], \mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}\} \cup \{\mathds{1}_d\},
nodes.label: eq: lin vectors

nodes.name: Constructed SEM is positive
nodes.statement: The SEM constructed above belongs to $\mathbb{M}^+(\mathcal{G}')$.
conclusions: The SEM constructed above belongs to $\mathbb{M}^+(\mathcal{G}')$.

nodes.name: Theta entries equal on Gamma
conclusions: \theta_{i,j_1}(\mathbf{v}) = \theta_{i,j_2}(\mathbf{v}) = \cdots= \theta_{i,j_{\frac{\kappa+1}{2}}}(\mathbf{v}).
nodes.statement_short: In the constructed models, each theta_i(v) has equal entries at the indices of Gamma.

nodes.name: Hedge
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathbf{R}$ is a subset of observed variables $\mathbf{V}$. A hedge is a pair of $\mathbf{R}$-rooted c-forests $\langle \mathcal{F}, \mathcal{F}' \rangle$ such that $\mathcal{F}'$ is a subgraph of $\mathcal{F}$.

nodes.name: Hedge in Figure 2
nodes.statement: \textbf{In Figure \ref{fig:countr_exmpl_complex}:} Subgraphs $\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{G}[\{R, T_1, T_2, T_3\}]$ and $\mathcal{F}' = \mathcal{G}[\{R\}]$ form a hedge $\langle \mathcal{F}, \mathcal{F}' \rangle$.

nodes.name: Maximal c-component partition C(G)
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{G})=\{\textbf{W}_i\}_{i=1}^{k}$, the set of c-components that partition observed variables in $\mathcal{G}$ such that each $\mathbf{W}_i$ is a maximal c-component. Maximal in the sense of number of nodes that is there is no $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbf{V}$ such that $\mathbf{W}_i \subsetneq \mathbf{W}$ and $\mathbf{W}$ is a c-component in $\mathcal{G}$.

nodes.name: Set T of a hedge
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathbf{T}$ is the set of all observed variables in $\mathcal{F}$ but not in $\mathcal{F}'$.

nodes.name: Subgraph F''
nodes.statement: We define $\mathcal{F}'':=\mathcal{F}[\textbf{T}]$.

nodes.name: C(G) and F'' in Figure 2
nodes.statement: \textbf{In Figure \ref{fig:countr_exmpl_complex}:} $\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{G}[\{T_1, T_2, T_3\}]) = \{ \{T_1, T_3\}, \{T_2\}\}$. Additionally, $\mathcal{F}'' = \mathcal{G}[\{T_1, T_2, T_3\}]$ for the hedge constructed before.

nodes.name: Hedgelet decomposition
nodes.statement:
Given a hedge $\langle \mathcal{F}, \mathcal{F}' \rangle$. Denote by $\mathbf{V}'$ a set of all observed variables of $\mathcal{F}'$. The hedgelet decomposition of a hedge $\langle \mathcal{F}, \mathcal{F}' \rangle$ is a collection of hedgelets $\{\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{W})\}_{\mathbf{W} \in \mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}'')}$ where each hedgelet $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{W})$ is a subgraph of $\mathcal{F}$ made of (i) $\mathcal{F}[\mathbf{W}\cup \mathbf{V}']$ and (ii) $\mathcal{F}[De_\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{W})]$ without bidirected edges, that is all observed descendants of $\mathbf{W}$ and all directed edges between them. 
            Let $\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{F}} := \{\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{W})\}_{\mathbf{W} \in \mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}'')}$ be the set of hedgelets of $\langle \mathcal{F}, \mathcal{F}' \rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Each maximal c-component W of F'' yields a hedgelet: F[W with F' variables] plus the directed descendants of W.

nodes.name: Hedgelets in Figure 2
nodes.statement: \textbf{In Figure \ref{fig:countr_exmpl_complex}:} For the hedge $\langle \mathcal{F}, \mathcal{F}' \rangle$, where $\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{G}[\{R, T_1, T_2, T_3\}]$ and $\mathcal{F}' = \mathcal{G}[\{R\}]$, there are two hedgelets $\mathcal{H}_1, \mathcal{H}_2$ displayed in Figures (\ref{subfig: hedgelet 1 exmpl 2})-(\ref{subfig: hedgelet 2 exmpl 2}). Moreover, we have $\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{F}} = \{\mathcal{H}_1, \mathcal{H}_2\}$.

nodes.name: Thicket
nodes.statement_short: A thicket is an R-rooted c-component built from a minimal c-component over R and one hedge per Z avoiding R.

nodes.name: Thicket formed for a causal effect
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ be disjoint sets of observed variables in $\mathcal{G}$. A thicket $\mathcal{J}$ is said to be formed for $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ in $\mathcal{G}$ with respect to $\mathbb{Z}$ if $\mathbf{R} \subseteq \Anc{\mathbf{Y}}{\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}]}$ and every hedgelet of each hedge $\langle \mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{Z}}, \mathcal{J}[\mathbf{R}]\rangle$ intersects with $\mathbf{X}$.
nodes.statement_short: A thicket is formed for P_x(y) if R lies in the ancestors of Y and every hedgelet of each hedge meets X.

nodes.name: Thicket in Figure 2
Set T of a thicket
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathbf{T}$ all observed variables in thicket $\mathcal{J}$ outside of subgraph $\mathcal{J}[\mathbf{R}]$.

nodes.name: Hedgelet collection H of a thicket
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{H} = \bigcup_{\{\langle \mathcal{F}, \mathcal{F}'\rangle \}\in \mathbb{F}_{\mathcal{J}}}\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{F}}$, that is, a collection of all hedgelets induced by the hedges of $\mathcal{J}$.

nodes.name: T and H in Figure 2
nodes.statement: \textbf{In Figure \ref{fig:countr_exmpl_complex}:} $\mathbf{T} = \{T_1, T_2, T_3\}$ and $\mathbb{H} = \{\mathcal{H}_1, \mathcal{H}_2\}$.

nodes.name: Lemma 3 of Lee et al. (zero root variable)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{T}'\subsetneq \mathbf{T}$ such that there exists a hedgelet $\mathcal{H} \in \mathbb{H}\setminus\mathbb{H}(\mathbf{T}')$, where $\mathbb{H}(\mathbf{T}')$ is a set of hedgelets from $\mathbb{H}$ which contain at least one variable from $\textbf{T}'$. Then, under the intervention $do(\mathbf{t}')$, there exists $R \in \mathbf{R}$, for any instantiation of $\mathbf{U}$, such that $r=0$ in both models.
assumptions: $\mathbf{T}'\subsetneq \mathbf{T}$ such that there exists a hedgelet $\mathcal{H} \in \mathbb{H}\setminus\mathbb{H}(\mathbf{T}')$
conclusions: under the intervention $do(\mathbf{t}')$, there exists $R \in \mathbf{R}$, for any instantiation of $\mathbf{U}$, such that $r=0$ in both models
nodes.statement_short: If some hedgelet avoids T', then under do(t') some root R is 0 in both of Lee et al.'s models.

nodes.name: Lee et al. models violate positivity
nodes.statement:
Note that by the construction in \citep{lee2019general}, $R$ in the above Lemma is a binary random variable. 
        In the above Lemma, let $\mathbf{T}' = \varnothing$. 
        Based on this Lemma, for any instantiation of unobserved variables $\mathbf{U}$, $P(\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{v})=0$, where $\textbf{v}$ is a realization for observed variables in which $r=1$. 
        This clearly shows that the constructed models in \citep{lee2019general} violate the positivity assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Taking T' empty in Lemma 3 gives P(v)=0 whenever r=1, so Lee et al.'s models are not positive.

nodes.name: Lee et al. models for the thicket of Figure 2
nodes.section: A.3 On the relaxed positivity assumption
nodes.statement_short: Spells out Lee et al.'s binary/vector models on the Fig. 2 thicket, which violate relaxed positivity.

nodes.name: Ancestral set
nodes.statement: We say a subset $\mathbf{X}$ of observed variables $\mathbf{V}$ is ancestral in $\mathcal{G}$, if $\mathbf{X} = \Anc{\mathbf{X}}{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V}}}$.

nodes.name: Marginalization of Q over ancestral sets
conclusions: Q[\mathbf{W}] = \sum_{\mathbf{C} \setminus \mathbf{W}}Q[\mathbf{C}].
nodes.statement_short: Q of an ancestral subset W of C is the marginal of Q[C] over C\W.
nodes.label: lemma: Q-marginal

nodes.name: Edge deletion from X preserves g-identifiability of Q[X]
nodes.statement:
Consider a causal graph $\mathcal{G}$ with observed variables $\mathbf{V}$.
            Suppose $\mathbf{X} \subseteq \mathbf{V}$ and $e:=(X_1,Z)$ is a directed edge such that $X_1\in\mathbf{X}$.
            
            $Q[\mathbf{X}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$ if and only if $Q[\mathbf{X}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{H})$, where $\mathcal{H}$ is the graph obtained by deleting $e$ from $\mathcal{G}$.
assumptions: $\mathbf{X} \subseteq \mathbf{V}$ and $e:=(X_1,Z)$ is a directed edge such that $X_1\in\mathbf{X}$
conclusions: $Q[\mathbf{X}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$ if and only if $Q[\mathbf{X}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{H})$
nodes.statement_short: Deleting a directed edge out of X does not change g-identifiability of Q[X].
nodes.label: lemma: prp3 - 1

nodes.name: Proof of edge-deletion lemma
nodes.statement:
$\mathbf{X}$ has the same c-components in $\mathcal{G}$ and $\mathcal{H}$ since $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V}}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{V}}$ have the same undirected edges. 
            Let $\mathbf{X}_1,\cdots,\mathbf{X}_l$ be the c-components of $\mathbf{X}$. 
            For any $i\in [1:l]$ and $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{A}$ such that $\mathbf{X}_i \subseteq \mathbf{A}$, \cite{huang2008completeness} showed that $Q[\mathbf{X}_i]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]$ if and only if $Q[\mathbf{X}_i]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{H}[\mathbf{A}]$. 
            Hence, Theorem \ref{thm: main} implies that $Q[\mathbf{X}_i]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$ if and only if $Q[\mathbf{X}_i]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{H})$.
            In this case, Proposition \ref{prp: 4} implies that $Q[\mathbf{X}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$ if and only if $Q[\mathbf{X}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{H})$.
nodes.statement_short: c-components are unchanged; Huang-Valtorta's per-A equivalence plus Theorem 1 and Proposition 4 transfer g-identifiability.

nodes.name: Adding an edge inside Y preserves non-g-identifiability
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are disjoint subsets of $\mathbf{V}$. Let $(Y_1,Y_2)$ (i.e., $Y_1\rightarrow Y_2$) denotes a directed edge in $\mathcal{G}$, where $Y_1,Y_2 \in \mathbf{Y}$. Let $\mathcal{G}'$ denotes the resulting graph after removing edge $(Y_1,Y_2)$ from $\mathcal{G}$. If the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}')$, then the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y} \setminus \{Y_1\}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
assumptions: $(Y_1,Y_2)$ (i.e., $Y_1\rightarrow Y_2$) denotes a directed edge in $\mathcal{G}$, where $Y_1,Y_2 \in \mathbf{Y}$
the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}')$
conclusions: the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y} \setminus \{Y_1\}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$
nodes.statement_short: If P_x(y) is not g-identifiable without edge Y1->Y2, then P_x(y\{y1}) is not g-identifiable with it.
nodes.label: lemma: prp3 - 2

nodes.name: Proof of edge-addition lemma
nodes.statement:
Herein, we provide a proof that is similar to one of the proofs in \citep{huang2008completeness}.
            
            Using Markov factorization property in graph $\mathcal{G}'$, $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is given by
            \begin{equation*}
                P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}) = 
                \sum_{\mathbf{V}\setminus(\mathbf{X}\cup \mathbf{Y})} \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{W \in \mathbf{V}\setminus \mathbf{X}}P(w \mid \Pa{W}{\mathcal{G}'}) \prod_{U \in \mathbf{U}} P(u).
            \end{equation*}
            Similarly, in graph $\mathcal{G}$ we have
            \begin{equation*}
                P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y} \setminus\{Y_1\}) = 
                \sum_{\{Y_1\} \cup (\mathbf{V} \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y}))} \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{W \in \mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}} P(w \mid \Pa{W}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U \in \mathbf{U}} P(u).
            \end{equation*}
            Since the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}')$, there exists $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$ in $\mathbb{M}^+(\mathcal{G}')$ such that:
            \begin{equation*}
                Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}),\; \forall \mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}},\; \forall i \in [0: m],
            \end{equation*}
            \begin{equation*}
                P_{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathcal{M}_1}(\mathbf{y})\neq P_{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathcal{M}_2}(\mathbf{y}),\; \exists \mathbf{x} \in \dom{\mathbf{X}}, \; \exists \mathbf{y} \in \dom{\mathbf{Y}}.
            \end{equation*}
            Using $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$, we construct two SEMs $\mathcal{M}_1'$ and $\mathcal{M}_2'$ in $\mathbb{M}^+(\mathcal{G})$. 
            Define a surjective function $F\!:\: \dom{Y_1}\rightarrow \{0, 1\}$ and a function $\Psi \!:\: \{0, 1\}\times \dom{Y_1} \rightarrow (0,1)$ such that $\Psi(0, y_1)+\Psi(1, y_1)=1$ for each $y_1 \in \dom{Y_1}$.
            We will later assume some constraints for these functions, but for now lets assume they are arbitrary. 
            
            For any node $S$ which is either unobserved or in $\mathbf{V} \setminus (\{Y_2\}\cup \Ch{Y_2}{\mathcal{G}})$, we define
            \begin{equation*}
                P^{\mathcal{M}_i'}(s|\Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}}) = P^{\mathcal{M}_i}(s|\Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'}),
            \end{equation*}
            where $i \in \{1, 2\}$.
            The domain of $Y_2$ in $\mathcal{M}_i'$ is defined as $\dom{Y_2}^{\mathcal{M}}\times \{0, 1\}$, where $\dom{Y_2}^{\mathcal{M}}$ is the domain of $Y_2$ in $\mathcal{M}_i$. 
            For $y_2 \in \dom{Y_2}^{\mathcal{M}}$, $i\in \{0,1\}$, and $k\in \{0, 1\}$ we define:
            \begin{equation*}
                P^{\mathcal{M}_i'}((y_2, k) 
                \mid \Pa{Y_2}{\mathcal{G}'}, y_1) =
                P^{\mathcal{M}_i}(y_2 \mid \Pa{Y_2}{\mathcal{G}'}) \Psi(F(y_1)\oplus k, y_1).
            \end{equation*}
            Note that $\Pa{Y_2}{\mathcal{G}'}\cup \{Y_1\}= \Pa{Y_2}{\mathcal{G}}$.
            Moreover, for a fixed realization $(\Pa{Y_2}{\mathcal{G}'}, y_1)$, we have:
            \begin{equation*}
                \sum_{k\in \{0,1\}} \sum_{y_2\in \dom{Y_2}^{\mathcal{M}}} P^{\mathcal{M}_i'}((y_2, k)|pa(Y_2), y_1) = 1.
            \end{equation*}
            
            For each $S \in \Ch{Y_2}{\mathcal{G}}$, we define:
            \begin{equation*}
                P^{\mathcal{M}_i'}(s \mid \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}}\setminus \{Y_2\}, (y_2, k)) =
                P^{\mathcal{M}_i}(s \mid \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}}\setminus \{Y_2\}, y_2).
            \end{equation*}
            
            Next, we show that $Q^{\mathcal{M}_1'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v})$ for each $\mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}}$ and $i \in [0:m]$.
            Suppose $\mathbf{v}$ is a realization of $\mathbf{V}$ in $\mathcal{M}'_1$ with realizations $y_1$ and $(y_2, k)$ for $Y_1$ and $Y_2$, respectively. 
            Consider two cases: 
            \begin{itemize}
                \item If $Y_2 \notin \mathbf{A}_i$:
                \begin{align*}
                    Q^{\mathcal{M}_1'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) 
                    &= \sum_{\mathbf{U}}\prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}})\prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}}P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(u) \\
                    & = \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i}P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}'})\prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(u) 
                    = Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) 
                    = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) \\
                    & = \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}'}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(u) \\
                    &= \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(u) \\ 
                    &= Q^{\mathcal{M}_2'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}).
                \end{align*}
                \item If $Y_2 \in \mathbf{A}_i$:
                \begin{align*}
                    Q^{\mathcal{M}_1'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) 
                    &= \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'} (a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}})\prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(u) \\
                    & = \Psi\left(F(y_1)\oplus k, y_1\right) \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(a \mid  \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}'}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}}P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(u) \\
                    &= \Psi(F(y_1)\oplus k, y_1) Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = \Psi(F(y_1)\oplus k, y_1) Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) \\
                    &= \Psi(F(y_1)\oplus k, y_1) \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{M_2}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}'}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{M_2}(u) \\
                    &= \sum_{\mathbf{U}}\prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}})) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}}P^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(u) \\
                    &= Q^{\mathcal{M}_2'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}).
                \end{align*}
            \end{itemize}
            Therefore, $Q^{\mathcal{M}_1'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v})$ for each $\mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}}$ and $i \in [0:m]$.
            
            We know that there exists $\hat{\mathbf{x}} \in \dom{\mathbf{X}}^{\mathcal{M}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{y}} \in \dom{\mathbf{Y}}^{\mathcal{M}}$ such that $P^{\mathcal{M}_1}_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}})\neq P^{\mathcal{M}_2}_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}})$. 
            Denote by $\hat{y}_1$ and $\hat{y}_2$ the realizations of $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ in the realization $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, respectively. 
            Assume that $P^{\mathcal{M}_1}_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}) = d_1 > P^{\mathcal{M}_2}_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}) = d_2$. 
            Assume that $\Psi(F(\hat{y}_1)\oplus 0, \hat{y}_1)=0.5$ and $\Psi(F(y)\oplus 0, y) = \frac{d_1-d_2}{4}$ for all $y \in \dom{Y_1}\setminus \{\hat{y}_1\}$. 
            Then we have:
            \begin{align*}
                P_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(\hat{\mathbf{y}} \setminus \{\hat{y}_1\})
                &=\sum_{y_1 \in \dom{Y_1}} \sum_{\mathbf{V} \setminus (\mathbf{X}\cup\mathbf{Y})} \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{Z\in \mathbf{V}\setminus \mathbf{X}} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(z \mid \Pa{Z}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P(u) \\
                & >\sum_{y_1 = \hat{y}_1} \sum_{\mathbf{V}\setminus (\mathbf{X}\cup\mathbf{Y})} \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{Z\in \mathbf{V}\setminus \mathbf{X}} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(z \mid \Pa{Z}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P(u) \\
                & =P_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{\mathcal{M}_1}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}) \Psi(F(\hat{y}_1)\oplus 0, \hat{y}_1) = 0.5 d_1.
            \end{align*}
            but, 
            \begin{align*}
                P_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(\hat{\mathbf{y}} \setminus \{\hat{y}_1\})
                &=\sum_{y_1 \in \dom{Y_1}} \sum_{\mathbf{V} \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y})} \sum_{\mathbf{U}}  \prod_{Z\in \mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(z \mid \Pa{Z}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P(u)\\
                & =\sum_{y_1 = \hat{y}_1} \sum_{\mathbf{V} \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y} )} \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{Z\in \mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(z \mid \Pa{Z}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P(u) \\
                & + \sum_{y_1 \in \dom{Y_1}\setminus \{\hat{y}_1\}} \sum_{\mathbf{V} \setminus (\mathbf{X}\cup\mathbf{Y})} \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{Z\in \mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}} P^{M_1'}(z \mid \Pa{Z}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U \in \mathbf{U}} P(u) \\
                &\leq P_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{\mathcal{M}_2}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}) \Psi(F(\hat{y}_1)\oplus 0, \hat{y}_1) + P_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{\mathcal{M}_2}(\hat{\mathbf{y}} \setminus \{\hat{y}_1\}) \Psi(F(Y_1\neq y_1)\oplus 0, Y_1\neq y_1)\\
                & = 0.5d_2 + \frac{d_1-d_2}{4} < 0.5d_1.
            \end{align*}
            This implies that $P_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(\hat{\mathbf{y}} \setminus \{\hat{y}_1\})\neq P_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(\hat{\mathbf{y}} \setminus \{\hat{y}_1\})$ which concludes the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of reduction lemma
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{X}:=\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{W}$. 
            
            \textit{Sufficient part}:
            Suppose $Q[\mathbf{W}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
            Since $Q[\mathbf{W}] = P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{W})$, we have
            \begin{equation*}
                P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_{\mathbf{W} \setminus \mathbf{Y}} Q[\mathbf{W}].
            \end{equation*}
            Hence, $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is uniquely computed and the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$. 
            
            \textit{Necessary part:} 
            Suppose $Q[\mathbf{W}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$, we will show that $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is also not g-identifiable. 
            To this end, first, we order the nodes in $\mathbf{W} \setminus \mathbf{Y}$, say $(W_1, W_2, \cdots, W_n)$, such that for each $1\leq i \leq n$, $W_i$ is a parent of at least one node in $\mathbf{Y}\cup \{W_1, W_2, \dots, W_{i-1}\}$. 
            Assume that $e_i$ is the directed edge from $W_i$ to its child in $\mathbf{Y}\cup \{W_1, W_2, \dots, W_{i-1}\}$.
            We also define $\mathcal{G}'$ to be the graph obtained by deleting all the edges $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^n$ from $\mathcal{G}$. 
            Applying Lemma \ref{lemma: prp3 - 1} repeatedly $n$ times imply that $Q[\mathbf{W}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},  \mathcal{G}')$.
            
            Let $\mathcal{G}_n:=\mathcal{G}$ and for $0\leq i\leq n-1$, we define $\mathcal{G}_i$ to be the graph obtained by removing $e_{i+1}$ from $\mathcal{G}_{i+1}$.
            From Lemma \ref{lemma: prp3 - 2}, we know that if $Q[\mathbf{W}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}')$, then adding edge $e_1$ will make the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{W} \setminus \{W_1\}$ not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}_1)$.
            Note that $\mathcal{G}_1$ is obtained from $\mathcal{G}'$ by adding edge $e_1$. 
            Using this lemma again implies that the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{W} \setminus \{W_1, W_2\}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}_2)$. 
            Repeating this procedure yields that the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{W} \setminus \{W_1, \dots W_n\}=\mathbf{Y}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}_n)$. 
            Since $\mathcal{G}_n=\mathcal{G}$, the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.

nodes.statement:
By the construction, it is clear that the model belongs to $\mathbb{M}(\mathcal{G}')$. 
        Hence, we need to show that $P(\mathbf{v})>0$ for any $\mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$. 
        To this end, it is enough to show that for any realization $\mathbf{v} \in \dom{\mathbf{V}}'$, there exists a realization $\hat{\mathbf{u}}\in \dom{\mathbf{U}'}$ such that $P(\mathbf{v}, \hat{\mathbf{u}})>0$, because in this case we have
        \begin{equation*}
            P(\mathbf{v}) = \sum_{\mathbf{u}=\dom{\mathbf{U}'}} P(\mathbf{v,u}) \geq P(\mathbf{v}, \hat{\mathbf{u}}) > 0.
        \end{equation*}
        Let $\mathbf{v}$ be a fixed realization in $\dom{\mathbf{V}'}$. 
        For the rest of the proof, we assume all the realizations for $\mathbf{V}'$ are consistent with $\mathbf{v}$.
        
        By Markov factorization property,  for any $\mathbf{u}\in \dom{\mathbf{U}'}$ we have 
        \begin{equation}
            P(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u}) = \prod_{V\in \mathbf{V}'}P(v\mid \Pa{V}{\mathcal{G}'})\prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}'}P(u).
        \end{equation}
        By the construction of our model, we have $P(u)>0$ for any $U\in \mathbf{U}'$ and $u\in \dom{U}$. 
        Moreover, for any $X\in \mathbf{S}$ and any realization for $\Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}'}\cap \mathbf{U}'$ we have $P(x \mid \Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}'})>0$. 
        Hence, it is enough to show that there exists $\hat{\mathbf{u}}\in \dom{\mathbf{U}'}$ such that $P(x \mid \Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}'})>0$ for each $X\in \mathbf{T}$.
        
        Recall that for each $X\in \mathbf{T}$, we have $X=(X[i_1],\cdots, X[i_{\alpha(X)}])$, where $X$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}_{i_1}, \cdots, \mathcal{F}_{i_{\alpha(X)}}$ and 
        \begin{equation*}
            X[i_j] \equiv \left(\sum_{Y \in \Pa{X}{\mathcal{F}_{i_j}}} Y[i_j]\right) \pmod{2}.
        \end{equation*}
        
        By the construction, we define the entries corresponding to each $\mathcal{F}_i$ separately. 
        For each $i\in [0:k]$, let $\mathbf{U}_i$ to be the set of unobserved variables in $\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{T}}$ that are in $\mathcal{F}_i$. 
        
        Let us fix an $i\in [0:k]$. 
        To finish the prove, we will introduce a method to determine $\hat{u}[i]$ for each $U\in \mathbf{U}_i$ such that 
        \begin{equation} x[i] \equiv \left(\sum_{Y \in \Pa{X}{\mathcal{F}_{i}}} y[i]\right) \pmod{2},
        \end{equation}
        for each $X\in \mathbf{T} \cap \mathbf{B}_i$. 
        
        Lets start with an arbitrary set of values for $\{\hat{u}[i]\!:\: U\in \mathbf{U}_i\}$ which are either $0$ or $1$. 
        Suppose $X\in \mathbf{T} \cap \mathbf{B}_i$. 
        We introduce a trick such that $x[i]$ will be replaced by $1- x[i]$ while for all $Y\in \mathbf{T} \cap \mathbf{B}_i$, $y[i]$ remains the same: \\
        By the construction of $\mathcal{F}_i$, there exists a path $(X=X_1, U_1, X_2, \cdots, X_l,U_l,Z = X_{l+1} )$ from $X$ to a variable $Z \in \mathbf{S}$ such that $\{U_1, \cdots, U_l\} \subseteq \mathbf{U}_i$, $\{X_1,\cdots,X_l\} \subseteq \mathbf{B}_i \cap \mathbf{T}$, and $\Ch{U_j}{\mathcal{F}_i} = \{X_j, X_{j+1}\}$ for each $j\in [1:l]$. 
        Now for each $j \in [1:l]$, we replace $\hat{u}_j[i]$ by $1-\hat{u}_j[i]$. 
        Since Equation \eqref{eq: eq for T} is in mod $2$, the value of $x_j[i]$ will be the same for each $j\in [2:l]$ while $x[i]$ will be replaced by $1-x[i]$. 
        Note that $X_{l+1}=Z \notin \mathbf{T}$. 
        
        With the trick described above, we can construct any realization for the $i$-th bit of the variables in $\mathbf{T} \cap \mathbf{B}_i$. 
        Hence, we can construct $\hat{\mathbf{u}}\in \dom{\mathbf{U}'}$ such that $P(x \mid \Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}'})>0$ for each $X\in \mathbf{T}$.
