nodes.name: Overview
nodes.statement:
In this section, we present the main steps of the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: main}.
    The technical lemmas in this section are proved in Appendix \ref{sec: apd_proof}.
nodes.statement_short: Outline: technical lemmas are proved in the appendix.

nodes.name: Sufficient part
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{Sufficient part:}
    This part is straightforward: if $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]$ for some $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{A}$ such that $\mathbf{S} \subseteq \mathbf{A}$, then $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is uniquely computable from $Q[\mathbf{A}]$, and therefore, $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$.
nodes.statement_short: Identifiability from G[A] makes Q[S] computable from Q[A].

nodes.name: Necessary part
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{Necessary part:}
    Suppose $\mathbf{S}$ is a single c-component and  $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not identifiable from $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}_i]$ for all $\mathbf{A}_i \in \mathbb{A}$ such that $\mathbf{S} \subseteq \mathbf{A}_i$. 
    We need to show that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$.
    Recall that $\mathbb{A}=\{\mathbf{A}_i\}_{i=0}^m$.
    To this end, we will introduce two SEMs $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$ in $\mathbb{M^+(\mathcal{G})}$ such that for each $i\in [0:m]$ and any $\mathbf{v} \in \dom{\mathbf{V}}$,
    \begin{equation} Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}), 
    \end{equation}
    but there exists $\mathbf{v}_0 \in \dom{\mathbf{V}}$ such that 
    \begin{equation} Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}_0) \neq Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}_0).
    \end{equation}
    This shows that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ cannot be uniquely computed from $\{Q[\mathbf{A}_i]\}_{i=0}^m$.
    
    For sake of space, we assume that there exists at least one $i\in [0, m]$ such that $\mathbf{S}\subset \mathbf{A}_i$. 
    In this case, without loss of generality, we assume that there exists $k \in [0:m]$ such that  $\mathbf{S}\subset \mathbf{A}_i$ for $i\in [0:k]$ and $\mathbf{S}\nsubseteq \mathbf{A}_i$ for $i\in [k+1:m]$.
    A proof for the case in which $\mathbf{S}$ is not a subset of $\mathbf{A}_i$ for all $i\in [0, m]$ is provided in Appendix \ref{sec: apd_second case}.
    
    We first modify $\mathcal{G}$ by deleting some nodes and edges and show that it is enough to prove Theorem \ref{thm: main} for the modified graph. 
    Then, we provide our method for constructing $\mathcal{M}_2$ from $\mathcal{M}_1$ by introducing a system of linear equations.
nodes.statement_short: Set up two positive SEMs agreeing on all Q[A_i] but differing on Q[S].

nodes.name: Goal of necessity
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{Necessary part:}
    Suppose $\mathbf{S}$ is a single c-component and  $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not identifiable from $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}_i]$ for all $\mathbf{A}_i \in \mathbb{A}$ such that $\mathbf{S} \subseteq \mathbf{A}_i$. 
    We need to show that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$.
    Recall that $\mathbb{A}=\{\mathbf{A}_i\}_{i=0}^m$.
nodes.statement_short: State the contrapositive goal.

nodes.name: Two witnessing SEMs
nodes.statement:
To this end, we will introduce two SEMs $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$ in $\mathbb{M^+(\mathcal{G})}$ such that for each $i\in [0:m]$ and any $\mathbf{v} \in \dom{\mathbf{V}}$,
    \begin{equation} Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}), 
    \end{equation}
    but there exists $\mathbf{v}_0 \in \dom{\mathbf{V}}$ such that 
    \begin{equation} Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}_0) \neq Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}_0).
    \end{equation}
    This shows that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ cannot be uniquely computed from $\{Q[\mathbf{A}_i]\}_{i=0}^m$.
nodes.statement_short: Need M1, M2 satisfying (6) and (7).

nodes.name: WLOG some A_i contains S
nodes.statement:
For sake of space, we assume that there exists at least one $i\in [0, m]$ such that $\mathbf{S}\subset \mathbf{A}_i$. 
    In this case, without loss of generality, we assume that there exists $k \in [0:m]$ such that  $\mathbf{S}\subset \mathbf{A}_i$ for $i\in [0:k]$ and $\mathbf{S}\nsubseteq \mathbf{A}_i$ for $i\in [k+1:m]$.
    A proof for the case in which $\mathbf{S}$ is not a subset of $\mathbf{A}_i$ for all $i\in [0, m]$ is provided in Appendix \ref{sec: apd_second case}.
nodes.statement_short: Order the A_i so that the first k+1 contain S; other case in Appendix C.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement:
We first modify $\mathcal{G}$ by deleting some nodes and edges and show that it is enough to prove Theorem \ref{thm: main} for the modified graph. 
    Then, we provide our method for constructing $\mathcal{M}_2$ from $\mathcal{M}_1$ by introducing a system of linear equations.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: simplify graph, then reduce to linear equations.

nodes.name: Graph modification
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{Graph modification:} Since $\mathbf{S}$ is single c-component, the bidirected edges in $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{S}}$ form a connected graph over $\mathbf{S}$. 
    Let $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}$ be a minimal (in terms of edges) spanning subgraph of $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{S}]$ such that $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{S}}$ is single c-component. 
    Thus, $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{S}}$ has no directed edges, and its bidirected edges form a spanning tree.
    \begin{lemma}[\cite{shpitser2006identification}] Suppose \mbox{$\mathbf{S} \subseteq\mathbf{A} \subseteq \mathbf{V}$}. 
        $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not identifiable from $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]$ if and only if there exists at least one $\mathbf{S}$-rooted c-forest  $\mathcal{F}$ with the set of observed variables $\mathbf{B}$ such that $\mathbf{S}\subsetneq \mathbf{B} \subseteq \mathbf{A}$, the bidirected edges of $\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{B}}$ form a spanning tree, and the induced subgraph of $\mathcal{F}$ over $\mathbf{S}$ is $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}$, i.e.,  $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}= \mathcal{F}[\mathbf{S}]$.
    \end{lemma}
    Recall that for each $i \in [0:k]$, $\mathbf{S}\subset \mathbf{A}_i$ and $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not identifiable from $Q[\mathbf{A}_i]$. 
    Hence, Lemma \ref{lem: c-forest existence} implies that for each $i\in [0:k]$, there exists a $\mathbf{S}$-rooted c-forest $\mathcal{F}_i$ over a set of observed variables $\mathbf{B}_i$ such that $\mathbf{S}\subsetneq \mathbf{B}_i \subseteq \mathbf{A}_i$, the bidirected edges of $(\mathcal{F}_i)_{\mathbf{S}}$ form a spanning tree, and $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}} = \mathcal{F}_i[\mathbf{S}]$. 
    Next, we use $\{\mathcal{F}_i\}_{i=0}^k$ to modify $\mathcal{G}$.

    We define $\mathcal{G}'$ to be the union of all the subgraphs in $\{\mathcal{F}_i\}_{i=0}^k$ with the observed variables $\mathbf{V}' := \bigcup_{i=0}^k \mathbf{B}_i$ and unobserved variables $\mathbf{U}'$.
    Furthermore, let $\mathbb{A}':= \{\mathbf{A}_i':=\mathbf{A}_i \cap \mathbf{V}'\}_{i=0}^m$. 
    Because for each $i\in [0:k]$, $\mathcal{F}_i$ is a $\mathbf{S}$-rooted c-forest in $\mathcal{G}'$, Lemma \ref{lem: c-forest existence} implies that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not identifiable from $\mathcal{G}'[\mathbf{A}_i']$.

    Next result establishes the connection between non g-identifiability of $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$ and non g-identifiability of $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ from $(\mathbb{A}', \mathcal{G}')$.
    \begin{lemma} If $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}', \mathcal{G}')$, then $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
    \end{lemma}
    To complete the proof using Lemma \ref{lem: simplify}, it is enough to show that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}', \mathcal{G}')$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace G by the union G' of S-rooted c-forests.

nodes.name: Spanning c-forest F^S
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{Graph modification:} Since $\mathbf{S}$ is single c-component, the bidirected edges in $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{S}}$ form a connected graph over $\mathbf{S}$. 
    Let $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}$ be a minimal (in terms of edges) spanning subgraph of $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{S}]$ such that $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{S}}$ is single c-component. 
    Thus, $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{S}}$ has no directed edges, and its bidirected edges form a spanning tree.
nodes.statement_short: Let F^S be a minimal spanning subgraph of G[S] that is a single c-component.

nodes.name: Cited c-forest lemma
nodes.statement_short: Quote the Shpitser-Pearl c-forest criterion.

nodes.name: c-forests F_i exist
nodes.statement:
Recall that for each $i \in [0:k]$, $\mathbf{S}\subset \mathbf{A}_i$ and $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not identifiable from $Q[\mathbf{A}_i]$. 
    Hence, Lemma \ref{lem: c-forest existence} implies that for each $i\in [0:k]$, there exists a $\mathbf{S}$-rooted c-forest $\mathcal{F}_i$ over a set of observed variables $\mathbf{B}_i$ such that $\mathbf{S}\subsetneq \mathbf{B}_i \subseteq \mathbf{A}_i$, the bidirected edges of $(\mathcal{F}_i)_{\mathbf{S}}$ form a spanning tree, and $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}} = \mathcal{F}_i[\mathbf{S}]$. 
    Next, we use $\{\mathcal{F}_i\}_{i=0}^k$ to modify $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 1 gives an S-rooted c-forest F_i inside each A_i, i<=k.

nodes.name: Define G' and A'
nodes.statement:
We define $\mathcal{G}'$ to be the union of all the subgraphs in $\{\mathcal{F}_i\}_{i=0}^k$ with the observed variables $\mathbf{V}' := \bigcup_{i=0}^k \mathbf{B}_i$ and unobserved variables $\mathbf{U}'$.
    Furthermore, let $\mathbb{A}':= \{\mathbf{A}_i':=\mathbf{A}_i \cap \mathbf{V}'\}_{i=0}^m$. 
    Because for each $i\in [0:k]$, $\mathcal{F}_i$ is a $\mathbf{S}$-rooted c-forest in $\mathcal{G}'$, Lemma \ref{lem: c-forest existence} implies that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not identifiable from $\mathcal{G}'[\mathbf{A}_i']$.
nodes.statement_short: G' is the union of the F_i; Q[S] stays non-identifiable from G'[A_i'].

nodes.name: Simplification lemma
nodes.statement_short: State Lemma 2 transferring non-g-identifiability.

nodes.name: Reduced goal
nodes.statement: To complete the proof using Lemma \ref{lem: simplify}, it is enough to show that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}', \mathcal{G}')$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to treat (A', G').

nodes.name: Reduction to linear equations
nodes.statement_short: Models differ only in U_0's law; the agreement constraints become a linear system.

nodes.name: Goal on G'
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{From g-identifiability to a system of linear equations:} To show  that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}', \mathcal{G}')$, we introduce two models in $\mathbb{M^+(\mathcal{G}')}$ such that equations \eqref{eq: same Q over A} and \eqref{eq: diff Q over S} are satisfied. 
    That is, $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ cannot be uniquely computed from $\{Q[\mathbf{A}'_i]\}_{i=0}^m$.
nodes.statement_short: Need two models in M+(G') satisfying (6),(7).

nodes.name: Finite domains
nodes.statement:
Note that to define a SEM $\mathcal{M}$ over a causal graph $\mathcal{G}'$, it suffices to define the domains $\dom{X}$ and either the conditional distributions $P^{\mathcal{M}}(X|\Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}'})$ or the corresponding equation in the SEM for all  $X\in \mathbf{V}'\cup \mathbf{U}'$, where $\mathbf{V}'$ and $\mathbf{U}'$ denote the observed and unobserved variables in $\mathcal{G}'$. 
    We define the domains of all variables to be finite, i.e., $|\dom{X}|<\infty$ for all $X\in\mathbf{V}'\cup \mathbf{U}'$.
nodes.statement_short: An SEM is given by domains and conditionals; take finite domains.

nodes.name: Models differ only at U_0
nodes.statement:
Let $U_0 \in \mathbf{U}'$ be a fixed unobserved variable (we will discuss later how to select $U_0$) with domain $\dom{U_0} := \{\gamma_1,\cdots,\gamma_d\}$.
    We define both models $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$ to have similar distributions over all variables except variable $U_0$ (We will specify these distributions in Section \ref{sec: M1}.)
    More specifically, for all $V \in \mathbf{V}'$,
    \begin{equation} P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(V \mid \Pa{V}{\mathcal{G}'}) = P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(V \mid \Pa{V}{\mathcal{G}'}),
    \end{equation}
    and for all $U \in \mathbf{U}' \setminus \{U_0\}$,
    \begin{equation} P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(U) = P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(U)=\frac{1}{|\dom{U}|}.
    \end{equation}
    As the distributions in Equations \eqref{eq: same dist 1} and \eqref{eq: same dist 2} are the same for both models, for the sake of brevity, we drop the superscripts $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$ from here on.
    For $j\in[1:d]$, We define $P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(U_0=\gamma_j)=1/d$ and $P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(U_0 = \gamma_j)=p_j$, where we will specify $\{p_j\}_{j=1}^d$ later such that $\mathcal{M}_2\in\mathbb{M}^+(\mathcal{G}')$ and both Equations \eqref{eq: same Q over A} and \eqref{eq: diff Q over S} hold.
nodes.statement_short: Same conditionals everywhere except U_0: uniform in M1, p_j in M2.

nodes.name: theta and eta
nodes.statement_short: Define theta_{i,j}, eta_j and write Q[A_i'], Q[S] as their mixtures.

nodes.name: Linear system for p
nodes.statement_short: Substituting yields the linear system (10).

nodes.name: Equivalent beta system
nodes.statement_short: (10) is solvable iff the homogeneous system (11) is.

nodes.name: Rescaling remark
nodes.statement_short: Remark 3: beta solutions rescale to p solutions.

nodes.name: Need a sufficient condition
nodes.statement:
A solution to the system of linear equations in \eqref{eq: linear system 2} will specify the distribution of $U_0$ in model $\mathcal{M}_2$. Clearly, existence of a solution to \eqref{eq: linear system 2} depends on the choices of $\{\theta_{i,j}(\mathbf{v})\}$ and $\{\eta_j(\mathbf{v})\}$. 
    The following result presents a sufficient condition under which \eqref{eq: linear system 2} admits a solution.
nodes.statement_short: Solvability depends on theta, eta; a sufficient condition follows.

nodes.name: Linear-independence lemma
nodes.statement:
For $\mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$ and $i\in [0:m]$, let $\theta_i(\mathbf{v})$ and $\eta(\mathbf{v})$ denote the vectors $(\theta_{i,1}(\mathbf{v}),...,\theta_{i,d}(\mathbf{v}))$  and $(\eta_1(\mathbf{v}),...,\eta_d(\mathbf{v}))$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, respectively.
    \begin{lemma} Consider the following set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$
         \begin{equation} \mathbf{\Omega}:=\{\theta_{i}(\mathbf{v}):\ i\in [0:m], \mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}\} \cup \{\mathds{1}_d\},
        \end{equation}
        where $\mathds{1}_d$ denotes the all-ones vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$. 
        If there exists $\mathbf{v}_0 \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$ such that $\eta(\mathbf{v}_0)$ is linearly independent from all the vectors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$, then the system of linear equations in \eqref{eq: linear system 2} admits a solution. 
    \end{lemma}
nodes.statement_short: Define vectors theta_i(v), eta(v) and state Lemma 3.

nodes.name: Remaining tasks
nodes.statement:
To summarize, so far, we have introduced two models for proving the necessary part of Theorem \ref{thm: main}. 
    In order to complete the proof, it remains to specify the conditional distributions in \eqref{eq: same dist 1} for all observed variables which consequently specify the vectors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$ in Equation \eqref{eq: lin vectors} and to find a realization $\mathbf{v}_0 \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$ such that $\eta(\mathbf{v}_0)$ is linearly independent from the set of the vectors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to specify conditionals and find v_0.

nodes.name: Constructing the conditional distributions
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{Constructing the conditional distributions:} In order to specify the conditional distributions in \eqref{eq: same dist 1}, we first introduce the following definitions and notations. 
    
    Since $\mathbf{B}_0$ is a single c-component, the bidirected edges in $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{B}_0}'$ form a connected graph.
    Hence, there exists a bidirected edge between $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{B}_0 \setminus \mathbf{S}$.
    Accordingly, let $U_0$ be an unobserved variable in subgraph $\mathcal{F}_0$ that has one child in $\mathbf{S}$ and one child in $\mathbf{T} := \mathbf{V}' \setminus \mathbf{S}$.
    We denote the set of unobserved variables in $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{S}]$ by $\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}$ and define  $\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{T}} := \mathbf{U}' \setminus ( \mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}} \cup \{U_0\})$. 
    For $X \in \mathbf{V}' \cup \mathbf{U}'$, we define $\alpha(X)$ to denote the number of graphs in $\{\mathcal{F}_j\}_{j=0}^{k}$ that contains $X$.
    
    For each $i\in [0:k]$, let $T_i$ denotes a node in $\mathbf{B}_i \setminus \mathbf{S}$ such that $\Ch{T_i}{\mathcal{F}_i} \cap \mathbf{S} \neq \varnothing$. 
    Note that such variables exist because $\mathcal{F}_i$s are $\mathbf{S}$-rooted c-forest. 

    Now, we are ready to introduce the domains of all variables in $\mathbf{V}'\cup\mathbf{U}'$. Recall that $\mathbf{V}'=\textbf{S}\cup\mathbf{T}$ and $\mathbf{U}'=\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}} \cup \mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{T}} \cup \{U_0\}$.
    \begin{align*}
        &\dom{X} := [0:\kappa], \quad \forall X \in \mathbf{S},\\
        &\dom{X} := \{0, 1\}^{\alpha(T)}, \quad \forall X \in \mathbf{T},\\
        &\dom{X} := [0:\kappa], \quad \forall X \in \mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}},\\
        &\dom{X} := \{0, 1\}^{\alpha(U)}, \quad \forall X \in \mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{T}},\\
        &\dom{U_0} := [0:\kappa]\times\{0, 1\}^{\alpha(U_0)-1}.
    \end{align*}
    In the above definition, $\kappa$ is an arbitrary odd integer greater than $4$. 
    Note that the number of elements in $\dom{U_0}$ is $d=(\kappa+1)2^{\alpha(U_0)-1}$.

    According to the above definitions, for each $X\in \mathbf{T}\cup\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{T}}\cup \{U_0\}$, its domain $\dom{X}$ is a subset of  $\mathbb{R}^{\alpha(X)}$ and it belongs to exactly $\alpha(X)$ number of subgraphs in $\{\mathcal{F}_i\}_{i=0}^k$.
    Suppose $X$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}_{i_1},\cdots, \mathcal{F}_{i_{\alpha(X)}}$, where $i_1 < \cdots < i_{\alpha(X)}$.
    Thus, we denote $X$ by a vector $ (X[i_1],\cdots,X[i_{\alpha(X)}])$ of length $\alpha(X)$. Next, we construct the conditional distributions of the observed variables by specifying their functional dependencies to their parents.
        
    When $X\in \mathbf{T}$, we define the entries of its corresponding vector as
    \begin{equation*}
        X[i_j] \equiv \left(\sum_{Y \in \Pa{X}{\mathcal{F}_{i_j}}} Y[i_j]\right) \pmod{2},
    \end{equation*}
    where $j\in[1:\alpha(X)]$.
    
    We now construct the variables in $\mathbf{S}$. 
    Recall that $U_0$ has one child in $\mathbf{S}$ which we denote it by $S_0$.
    For each $S \in \mathbf{S}\setminus \{S_0\}$ and any realization of $\Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'}$, we define $\mathds{I}(S)$ to be one if there exists $i\in [0:k]$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $T_i \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'}$ and $T_i[i]=0$, or
        \item there exists $X \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'} \setminus (\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}\cup \{T_i\})$ such that $\mathcal{F}_i$ contains $X$ and $X[i]=1$,
    \end{enumerate}
    and zero, otherwise.
    Note that according to the definition of $T_i$, it belongs to $\mathcal{F}_i$ and therefore, $T_i[i]$ exists. 
    Analogously, we define $\mathds{I}(S_0)$ to be one if there exists $i\in [0:k]$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $T_i \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'}$ and $T_i[i]=0$, or
        \item $i\neq0$, $\mathcal{F}_i$ contains $U_0$, and $U_0[i]=1$, or
        \item there exists $X \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'} \setminus (\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}\cup \{T_i,U_0\})$ such that $\mathcal{F}_i$ contains $X$ and $X[i]=1$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    Now, for each $S\in \mathbf{S}$ and $s \in [0:\kappa]$, we define $P(S=s \mid \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'})$ as
    \begin{equation*}
    \begin{cases} 
        \frac{1}{\kappa+1} & \text{ if } \mathds{I}(S)=1\\
        1-\kappa\epsilon &  \text{ if } \mathds{I}(S)=0  \text{ and } s \equiv M(S) \pmod{\kappa+1}, \\
        \epsilon &  \text{ if }  \mathds{I}(S)=0  \text{ and } s\not\equiv M(S) \pmod{\kappa+1},
    \end{cases}
    \end{equation*}
    where $0<\epsilon<\frac{1}{\kappa}$ and 
    \begin{equation*}
    M(S):=
    \begin{cases} 
        \sum_{x\in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'[\mathbf{S}]}}x & \text{, if } S\in \mathbf{S}\setminus \{S_0\}, \\
        u_0[0]+\sum_{x\in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'[\mathbf{S}]}}x & \text{, if $S=S_0$ }.
    \end{cases}
    \end{equation*}
    Note that $M(S)$ is an integer number. This is because $\Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'[\mathbf{S}]}\subseteq \mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}$ and thus all terms in the above definition belong to $[0:\kappa]$. 
    \begin{lemma} The SEM constructed above belongs to $\mathbb{M}^+(\mathcal{G}')$. 
    \end{lemma}
nodes.statement_short: Build the parity/mod-(kappa+1) model and state its positivity.

nodes.name: Choice of U_0 justified
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{Constructing the conditional distributions:} In order to specify the conditional distributions in \eqref{eq: same dist 1}, we first introduce the following definitions and notations. 
    
    Since $\mathbf{B}_0$ is a single c-component, the bidirected edges in $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{B}_0}'$ form a connected graph.
    Hence, there exists a bidirected edge between $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{B}_0 \setminus \mathbf{S}$.

nodes.name: Choose U_0 and T
nodes.statement: Accordingly, let $U_0$ be an unobserved variable in subgraph $\mathcal{F}_0$ that has one child in $\mathbf{S}$ and one child in $\mathbf{T} := \mathbf{V}' \setminus \mathbf{S}$.

nodes.name: U^S, U^T and alpha
nodes.statement:
We denote the set of unobserved variables in $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{S}]$ by $\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}$ and define  $\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{T}} := \mathbf{U}' \setminus ( \mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}} \cup \{U_0\})$. 
    For $X \in \mathbf{V}' \cup \mathbf{U}'$, we define $\alpha(X)$ to denote the number of graphs in $\{\mathcal{F}_j\}_{j=0}^{k}$ that contains $X$.

nodes.statement:
For each $i\in [0:k]$, let $T_i$ denotes a node in $\mathbf{B}_i \setminus \mathbf{S}$ such that $\Ch{T_i}{\mathcal{F}_i} \cap \mathbf{S} \neq \varnothing$. 
    Note that such variables exist because $\mathcal{F}_i$s are $\mathbf{S}$-rooted c-forest.

nodes.name: Domains
nodes.statement:
Now, we are ready to introduce the domains of all variables in $\mathbf{V}'\cup\mathbf{U}'$. Recall that $\mathbf{V}'=\textbf{S}\cup\mathbf{T}$ and $\mathbf{U}'=\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}} \cup \mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{T}} \cup \{U_0\}$.
    \begin{align*}
        &\dom{X} := [0:\kappa], \quad \forall X \in \mathbf{S},\\
        &\dom{X} := \{0, 1\}^{\alpha(T)}, \quad \forall X \in \mathbf{T},\\
        &\dom{X} := [0:\kappa], \quad \forall X \in \mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}},\\
        &\dom{X} := \{0, 1\}^{\alpha(U)}, \quad \forall X \in \mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{T}},\\
        &\dom{U_0} := [0:\kappa]\times\{0, 1\}^{\alpha(U_0)-1}.
    \end{align*}
    In the above definition, $\kappa$ is an arbitrary odd integer greater than $4$. 
    Note that the number of elements in $\dom{U_0}$ is $d=(\kappa+1)2^{\alpha(U_0)-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Domains: [0:kappa] for S-side, bit vectors for T-side.

nodes.name: Vector representation
nodes.statement:
According to the above definitions, for each $X\in \mathbf{T}\cup\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{T}}\cup \{U_0\}$, its domain $\dom{X}$ is a subset of  $\mathbb{R}^{\alpha(X)}$ and it belongs to exactly $\alpha(X)$ number of subgraphs in $\{\mathcal{F}_i\}_{i=0}^k$.
    Suppose $X$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}_{i_1},\cdots, \mathcal{F}_{i_{\alpha(X)}}$, where $i_1 < \cdots < i_{\alpha(X)}$.
    Thus, we denote $X$ by a vector $ (X[i_1],\cdots,X[i_{\alpha(X)}])$ of length $\alpha(X)$. Next, we construct the conditional distributions of the observed variables by specifying their functional dependencies to their parents.

nodes.name: T variables as parities
nodes.statement_short: Each coordinate of a T variable is the parity of its parents in that c-forest.

nodes.name: Indicator I(S)
nodes.statement:
We now construct the variables in $\mathbf{S}$. 
    Recall that $U_0$ has one child in $\mathbf{S}$ which we denote it by $S_0$.
    For each $S \in \mathbf{S}\setminus \{S_0\}$ and any realization of $\Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'}$, we define $\mathds{I}(S)$ to be one if there exists $i\in [0:k]$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $T_i \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'}$ and $T_i[i]=0$, or
        \item there exists $X \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'} \setminus (\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}\cup \{T_i\})$ such that $\mathcal{F}_i$ contains $X$ and $X[i]=1$,
    \end{enumerate}
    and zero, otherwise.
    Note that according to the definition of $T_i$, it belongs to $\mathcal{F}_i$ and therefore, $T_i[i]$ exists. 
    Analogously, we define $\mathds{I}(S_0)$ to be one if there exists $i\in [0:k]$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $T_i \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'}$ and $T_i[i]=0$, or
        \item $i\neq0$, $\mathcal{F}_i$ contains $U_0$, and $U_0[i]=1$, or
        \item there exists $X \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'} \setminus (\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}\cup \{T_i,U_0\})$ such that $\mathcal{F}_i$ contains $X$ and $X[i]=1$.
    \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Define the indicator I(S) of a 'noisy' configuration.

nodes.name: I(S) for S other than S_0
nodes.statement:
We now construct the variables in $\mathbf{S}$. 
    Recall that $U_0$ has one child in $\mathbf{S}$ which we denote it by $S_0$.
    For each $S \in \mathbf{S}\setminus \{S_0\}$ and any realization of $\Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'}$, we define $\mathds{I}(S)$ to be one if there exists $i\in [0:k]$ such that
nodes.statement_short: I(S)=1 if for some i one of the following holds.

nodes.name: Condition 1
nodes.statement: $T_i \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'}$ and $T_i[i]=0$, or
nodes.statement_short: T_i is a parent with bit 0.

nodes.name: Condition 2
nodes.statement_short: Another F_i parent has bit 1; otherwise I(S)=0.

nodes.name: I(S_0)
nodes.statement:
Note that according to the definition of $T_i$, it belongs to $\mathcal{F}_i$ and therefore, $T_i[i]$ exists. 
    Analogously, we define $\mathds{I}(S_0)$ to be one if there exists $i\in [0:k]$ such that
nodes.statement_short: Analogous indicator for S_0.

nodes.name: Condition 1 for S_0
nodes.statement: $T_i \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'}$ and $T_i[i]=0$, or
nodes.statement_short: T_i is a parent with bit 0.

nodes.name: Condition 2 for S_0
nodes.statement: $i\neq0$, $\mathcal{F}_i$ contains $U_0$, and $U_0[i]=1$, or
nodes.statement_short: U_0's i-th bit is 1 for i not 0.

nodes.name: Condition 3 for S_0
nodes.statement: there exists $X \in \Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'} \setminus (\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}\cup \{T_i,U_0\})$ such that $\mathcal{F}_i$ contains $X$ and $X[i]=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Another F_i parent has bit 1.

nodes.name: S conditionals
nodes.statement_short: S is uniform if I(S)=1, else concentrated at M(S) mod kappa+1 with eps noise.

nodes.name: Validity lemma
nodes.statement:
\begin{lemma} The SEM constructed above belongs to $\mathbb{M}^+(\mathcal{G}')$. 
    \end{lemma}
nodes.statement_short: State Lemma 4: model is positive.

nodes.name: Existence of realization v_0
nodes.statement_short: Theta is constant on Gamma but eta is not, so eta(v_0) is independent of Omega.

nodes.name: Subset Gamma
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{Existence of realization $\textbf{v}_0$:} Herein, we show that for the aforementioned conditional distributions, there exists a realization $\textbf{v}_0$ such that $\eta(\mathbf{v}_0)$ is linearly independent from the set of the vectors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$ (in Equation \eqref{eq: lin vectors}).  
    Consider the following subset of $\dom{U_0}=\{\gamma_1,...,\gamma_d\}$ with $\frac{\kappa+1}{2}$ elements:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathbf{\Gamma} := \Big\{(2x,0,\cdots,0)\!:\: x\in [0:\frac{\kappa-1}{2}]\Big\}.
    \end{equation*}
    Recall that for $\mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$ and $i\in[0:m]$, $\theta_i(\mathbf{v})$ and $\eta(\mathbf{v})$ are two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $j$-th entry corresponds to $U_0=\gamma_j$. 
    Suppose that $\mathbf{\Gamma}=\{\gamma_{j_1},...,\gamma_{j_{\frac{\kappa+1}{2}}}\}$. Next result shows that in our constructed models, all entries of $\theta_i(\textbf{v})$ with indices in $\{j_1,...,j_{\frac{\kappa+1}{2}}\}$ are equal.
nodes.statement_short: Define Gamma of even first-coordinate values of U_0.

nodes.name: Theta equal on Gamma
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5: theta entries coincide on Gamma, hence all of span(Omega).

nodes.name: Eta differs on Gamma
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6: eta(v_0) has two different entries on Gamma.

nodes.name: Conclude Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
Lemma \ref{lem: eta index} implies that there exist $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\epsilon$ for which there exists $\mathbf{v}_0 \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$ such that $\eta(\mathbf{v}_0)$ is linearly independent from the set of vectors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$.
    As we discussed before, this completes our proof for Theorem \ref{thm: main}.
nodes.statement_short: So eta(v_0) is independent of Omega and Lemma 3 finishes the proof.

nodes.name: Same c-components
nodes.statement: $\mathbf{X}$ has the same c-components in $\mathcal{G}$ and $\mathcal{H}$ since $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V}}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{V}}$ have the same undirected edges.
nodes.statement_short: Edge deletion leaves c-components unchanged.

nodes.name: Huang-Valtorta equivalence
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{X}_1,\cdots,\mathbf{X}_l$ be the c-components of $\mathbf{X}$. 
            For any $i\in [1:l]$ and $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{A}$ such that $\mathbf{X}_i \subseteq \mathbf{A}$, \cite{huang2008completeness} showed that $Q[\mathbf{X}_i]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]$ if and only if $Q[\mathbf{X}_i]$ is identifiable from $\mathcal{H}[\mathbf{A}]$.
nodes.statement_short: Per-A identifiability of each c-component is unchanged.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Hence, Theorem \ref{thm: main} implies that $Q[\mathbf{X}_i]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$ if and only if $Q[\mathbf{X}_i]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{H})$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1 transfers g-identifiability of each X_i.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 4
nodes.statement: In this case, Proposition \ref{prp: 4} implies that $Q[\mathbf{X}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$ if and only if $Q[\mathbf{X}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{H})$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 4 combines the c-components.

nodes.name: Proof template
nodes.statement: Herein, we provide a proof that is similar to one of the proofs in \citep{huang2008completeness}.
nodes.statement_short: Follow Huang-Valtorta's argument.

nodes.name: Factorize both effects
nodes.statement_short: Write P_x(y) in G' and P_x(y\{y1}) in G by Markov factorization.

nodes.name: Witness models in G'
nodes.statement_short: Take M1, M2 in M+(G') agreeing on Q[A_i] but differing on P_x(y).

nodes.name: Functions F and Psi
nodes.statement:
Using $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$, we construct two SEMs $\mathcal{M}_1'$ and $\mathcal{M}_2'$ in $\mathbb{M}^+(\mathcal{G})$. 
            Define a surjective function $F\!:\: \dom{Y_1}\rightarrow \{0, 1\}$ and a function $\Psi \!:\: \{0, 1\}\times \dom{Y_1} \rightarrow (0,1)$ such that $\Psi(0, y_1)+\Psi(1, y_1)=1$ for each $y_1 \in \dom{Y_1}$.
            We will later assume some constraints for these functions, but for now lets assume they are arbitrary.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce surjection F and weighting Psi.

nodes.name: Construct M1', M2'
nodes.statement_short: Copy conditionals; augment Y2 with a bit weighted by Psi(F(y1) xor k, y1); adapt children of Y2.

nodes.name: Agreement on Q[A_i]
nodes.statement:
Next, we show that $Q^{\mathcal{M}_1'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v})$ for each $\mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}}$ and $i \in [0:m]$.
            Suppose $\mathbf{v}$ is a realization of $\mathbf{V}$ in $\mathcal{M}'_1$ with realizations $y_1$ and $(y_2, k)$ for $Y_1$ and $Y_2$, respectively. 
            Consider two cases: 
            \begin{itemize}
                \item If $Y_2 \notin \mathbf{A}_i$:
                \begin{align*}
                    Q^{\mathcal{M}_1'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) 
                    &= \sum_{\mathbf{U}}\prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}})\prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}}P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(u) \\
                    & = \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i}P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}'})\prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(u) 
                    = Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) 
                    = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) \\
                    & = \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}'}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(u) \\
                    &= \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(u) \\ 
                    &= Q^{\mathcal{M}_2'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}).
                \end{align*}
                \item If $Y_2 \in \mathbf{A}_i$:
                \begin{align*}
                    Q^{\mathcal{M}_1'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) 
                    &= \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'} (a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}})\prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(u) \\
                    & = \Psi\left(F(y_1)\oplus k, y_1\right) \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(a \mid  \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}'}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}}P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(u) \\
                    &= \Psi(F(y_1)\oplus k, y_1) Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = \Psi(F(y_1)\oplus k, y_1) Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) \\
                    &= \Psi(F(y_1)\oplus k, y_1) \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{M_2}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}'}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{M_2}(u) \\
                    &= \sum_{\mathbf{U}}\prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}})) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}}P^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(u) \\
                    &= Q^{\mathcal{M}_2'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}).
                \end{align*}
            \end{itemize}
            Therefore, $Q^{\mathcal{M}_1'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v})$ for each $\mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}}$ and $i \in [0:m]$.
nodes.statement_short: The new models still agree on all available Q[A_i].

nodes.name: Fix realization
nodes.statement:
Next, we show that $Q^{\mathcal{M}_1'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v})$ for each $\mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}}$ and $i \in [0:m]$.
            Suppose $\mathbf{v}$ is a realization of $\mathbf{V}$ in $\mathcal{M}'_1$ with realizations $y_1$ and $(y_2, k)$ for $Y_1$ and $Y_2$, respectively. 
            Consider two cases:
nodes.statement_short: Fix v with values y1 and (y2,k).

nodes.name: Case Y2 not in A_i
nodes.statement:
If $Y_2 \notin \mathbf{A}_i$:
                \begin{align*}
                    Q^{\mathcal{M}_1'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) 
                    &= \sum_{\mathbf{U}}\prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}})\prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}}P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(u) \\
                    & = \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i}P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}'})\prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(u) 
                    = Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) 
                    = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) \\
                    & = \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}'}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(u) \\
                    &= \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(u) \\ 
                    &= Q^{\mathcal{M}_2'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}).
                \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Q[A_i] unchanged from the original models.

nodes.name: Case Y2 in A_i
nodes.statement:
If $Y_2 \in \mathbf{A}_i$:
                \begin{align*}
                    Q^{\mathcal{M}_1'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) 
                    &= \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'} (a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}})\prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(u) \\
                    & = \Psi\left(F(y_1)\oplus k, y_1\right) \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(a \mid  \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}'}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}}P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(u) \\
                    &= \Psi(F(y_1)\oplus k, y_1) Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = \Psi(F(y_1)\oplus k, y_1) Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) \\
                    &= \Psi(F(y_1)\oplus k, y_1) \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{M_2}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}'}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P^{M_2}(u) \\
                    &= \sum_{\mathbf{U}}\prod_{A\in \mathbf{A}_i} P^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(a \mid \Pa{A}{\mathcal{G}})) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}}P^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(u) \\
                    &= Q^{\mathcal{M}_2'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}).
                \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Q[A_i] picks up the common factor Psi.

nodes.name: Agreement holds
nodes.statement: Therefore, $Q^{\mathcal{M}_1'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2'}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v})$ for each $\mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}}$ and $i \in [0:m]$.
nodes.statement_short: Both cases give agreement.

nodes.name: Differing realization
nodes.statement:
We know that there exists $\hat{\mathbf{x}} \in \dom{\mathbf{X}}^{\mathcal{M}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{y}} \in \dom{\mathbf{Y}}^{\mathcal{M}}$ such that $P^{\mathcal{M}_1}_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}})\neq P^{\mathcal{M}_2}_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}})$. 
            Denote by $\hat{y}_1$ and $\hat{y}_2$ the realizations of $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ in the realization $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Fix x-hat, y-hat where the original effects differ.

nodes.name: Choose Psi
nodes.statement:
Assume that $P^{\mathcal{M}_1}_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}) = d_1 > P^{\mathcal{M}_2}_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}) = d_2$. 
            Assume that $\Psi(F(\hat{y}_1)\oplus 0, \hat{y}_1)=0.5$ and $\Psi(F(y)\oplus 0, y) = \frac{d_1-d_2}{4}$ for all $y \in \dom{Y_1}\setminus \{\hat{y}_1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG d1>d2; choose Psi values 0.5 and (d1-d2)/4.

nodes.name: Bound both effects
nodes.statement:
Then we have:
            \begin{align*}
                P_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(\hat{\mathbf{y}} \setminus \{\hat{y}_1\})
                &=\sum_{y_1 \in \dom{Y_1}} \sum_{\mathbf{V} \setminus (\mathbf{X}\cup\mathbf{Y})} \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{Z\in \mathbf{V}\setminus \mathbf{X}} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(z \mid \Pa{Z}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P(u) \\
                & >\sum_{y_1 = \hat{y}_1} \sum_{\mathbf{V}\setminus (\mathbf{X}\cup\mathbf{Y})} \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{Z\in \mathbf{V}\setminus \mathbf{X}} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(z \mid \Pa{Z}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P(u) \\
                & =P_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{\mathcal{M}_1}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}) \Psi(F(\hat{y}_1)\oplus 0, \hat{y}_1) = 0.5 d_1.
            \end{align*}
            but, 
            \begin{align*}
                P_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(\hat{\mathbf{y}} \setminus \{\hat{y}_1\})
                &=\sum_{y_1 \in \dom{Y_1}} \sum_{\mathbf{V} \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y})} \sum_{\mathbf{U}}  \prod_{Z\in \mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(z \mid \Pa{Z}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P(u)\\
                & =\sum_{y_1 = \hat{y}_1} \sum_{\mathbf{V} \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y} )} \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{Z\in \mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}} P^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(z \mid \Pa{Z}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}} P(u) \\
                & + \sum_{y_1 \in \dom{Y_1}\setminus \{\hat{y}_1\}} \sum_{\mathbf{V} \setminus (\mathbf{X}\cup\mathbf{Y})} \sum_{\mathbf{U}} \prod_{Z\in \mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}} P^{M_1'}(z \mid \Pa{Z}{\mathcal{G}}) \prod_{U \in \mathbf{U}} P(u) \\
                &\leq P_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{\mathcal{M}_2}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}) \Psi(F(\hat{y}_1)\oplus 0, \hat{y}_1) + P_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{\mathcal{M}_2}(\hat{\mathbf{y}} \setminus \{\hat{y}_1\}) \Psi(F(Y_1\neq y_1)\oplus 0, Y_1\neq y_1)\\
                & = 0.5d_2 + \frac{d_1-d_2}{4} < 0.5d_1.
            \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound for M1' and upper bound for M2'.

nodes.name: Effects differ
nodes.statement: This implies that $P_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{\mathcal{M}_1'}(\hat{\mathbf{y}} \setminus \{\hat{y}_1\})\neq P_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(\hat{\mathbf{y}} \setminus \{\hat{y}_1\})$ which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: The marginal effects differ, concluding the proof.

nodes.name: Notation X
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{X}:=\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{W}$.
nodes.statement_short: Set X = V\W.

nodes.name: Sufficient part
nodes.statement:
\textit{Sufficient part}:
            Suppose $Q[\mathbf{W}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
            Since $Q[\mathbf{W}] = P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{W})$, we have
            \begin{equation*}
                P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_{\mathbf{W} \setminus \mathbf{Y}} Q[\mathbf{W}].
            \end{equation*}
            Hence, $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is uniquely computed and the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
nodes.statement_short: Marginalize Q[W] to get P_x(y).

nodes.name: Necessary part
nodes.statement:
\textit{Necessary part:} 
            Suppose $Q[\mathbf{W}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$, we will show that $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is also not g-identifiable. 
            To this end, first, we order the nodes in $\mathbf{W} \setminus \mathbf{Y}$, say $(W_1, W_2, \cdots, W_n)$, such that for each $1\leq i \leq n$, $W_i$ is a parent of at least one node in $\mathbf{Y}\cup \{W_1, W_2, \dots, W_{i-1}\}$. 
            Assume that $e_i$ is the directed edge from $W_i$ to its child in $\mathbf{Y}\cup \{W_1, W_2, \dots, W_{i-1}\}$.
            We also define $\mathcal{G}'$ to be the graph obtained by deleting all the edges $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^n$ from $\mathcal{G}$. 
            Applying Lemma \ref{lemma: prp3 - 1} repeatedly $n$ times imply that $Q[\mathbf{W}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},  \mathcal{G}')$.
            
            Let $\mathcal{G}_n:=\mathcal{G}$ and for $0\leq i\leq n-1$, we define $\mathcal{G}_i$ to be the graph obtained by removing $e_{i+1}$ from $\mathcal{G}_{i+1}$.
            From Lemma \ref{lemma: prp3 - 2}, we know that if $Q[\mathbf{W}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}')$, then adding edge $e_1$ will make the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{W} \setminus \{W_1\}$ not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}_1)$.
            Note that $\mathcal{G}_1$ is obtained from $\mathcal{G}'$ by adding edge $e_1$. 
            Using this lemma again implies that the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{W} \setminus \{W_1, W_2\}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}_2)$. 
            Repeating this procedure yields that the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{W} \setminus \{W_1, \dots W_n\}=\mathbf{Y}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}_n)$. 
            Since $\mathcal{G}_n=\mathcal{G}$, the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
nodes.statement_short: Delete then re-add edges toward Y to propagate non-g-identifiability.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement:
\textit{Necessary part:} 
            Suppose $Q[\mathbf{W}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$, we will show that $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is also not g-identifiable.
nodes.statement_short: Assume Q[W] not g-identifiable.

nodes.name: Order and edges e_i
nodes.statement:
To this end, first, we order the nodes in $\mathbf{W} \setminus \mathbf{Y}$, say $(W_1, W_2, \cdots, W_n)$, such that for each $1\leq i \leq n$, $W_i$ is a parent of at least one node in $\mathbf{Y}\cup \{W_1, W_2, \dots, W_{i-1}\}$. 
            Assume that $e_i$ is the directed edge from $W_i$ to its child in $\mathbf{Y}\cup \{W_1, W_2, \dots, W_{i-1}\}$.
            We also define $\mathcal{G}'$ to be the graph obtained by deleting all the edges $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^n$ from $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: Order W\Y so each W_i has an edge e_i toward Y or earlier W's; delete them to get G'.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 9
nodes.statement: Applying Lemma \ref{lemma: prp3 - 1} repeatedly $n$ times imply that $Q[\mathbf{W}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},  \mathcal{G}')$.
nodes.statement_short: Q[W] stays non-g-identifiable in G'.

nodes.name: First re-addition
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{G}_n:=\mathcal{G}$ and for $0\leq i\leq n-1$, we define $\mathcal{G}_i$ to be the graph obtained by removing $e_{i+1}$ from $\mathcal{G}_{i+1}$.
            From Lemma \ref{lemma: prp3 - 2}, we know that if $Q[\mathbf{W}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}')$, then adding edge $e_1$ will make the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{W} \setminus \{W_1\}$ not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}_1)$.
            Note that $\mathcal{G}_1$ is obtained from $\mathcal{G}'$ by adding edge $e_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 10 after re-adding e_1 removes W_1 from the target.

nodes.name: Iterate
nodes.statement:
Using this lemma again implies that the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{W} \setminus \{W_1, W_2\}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}_2)$. 
            Repeating this procedure yields that the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{W} \setminus \{W_1, \dots W_n\}=\mathbf{Y}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G}_n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat for all e_i to reach target Y in G_n.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $\mathcal{G}_n=\mathcal{G}$, the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
nodes.statement_short: G_n = G, so P_x(y) is not g-identifiable.

nodes.name: Choose a basis
nodes.statement: Denote by $\{\phi_i\}_{i=1}^{l}$ a subset of $\{c_i\}_{i=1}^{n}$ which forms a basis for the vectors in $\{c_i\}_{i=1}^{n}$. Clearly, we have $l < d$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a basis phi of the c_i; l<d.

nodes.name: Linear system for b
nodes.statement_short: Set up <phi_i,b>=0, <c,b>=13.

nodes.name: Solvable
nodes.statement: By the assumption, vectors in $\{\phi_i\}_{i=1}^{l}\cup\{c\}$ are linearly independent, thus there exists a solution to \eqref{eq: lem11}.
nodes.statement_short: Linear independence gives a solution.

nodes.name: Marginalization identity
nodes.statement_short: Marginalize Q[V\X] and apply Lemma 8 to get P_x(y) from Q[W].

nodes.name: Sufficient part
nodes.statement_short: Equation (16) computes P_x(y) from Q[W].

nodes.name: Necessary part
nodes.statement:
\textit{Necessary part:}
            Suppose $Q[\mathbf{W}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$. 
            For each $W \in \mathbf{W} \setminus \mathbf{Y}$, there exists a directed path in $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{W}]$ from $W$ to a variable in $\mathbf{Y}$. 
            Hence, Lemma \ref{lemma: prp3 - 3} implies that the causal effect of $\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{W}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$. 
            Hence, Equation \eqref{eq: prp 3 proof} implies that $ P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ cannot be uniquely computed and the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 11 and (16) give non-g-identifiability of P_x(y).

nodes.name: Assume and note paths
nodes.statement_short: Assume Q[W] not g-identifiable; each W\Y node reaches Y.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 11
nodes.statement: Hence, Lemma \ref{lemma: prp3 - 3} implies that the causal effect of $\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{W}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
nodes.statement_short: P_{v\w}(y) is not g-identifiable.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence, Equation \eqref{eq: prp 3 proof} implies that $ P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ cannot be uniquely computed and the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A},\mathcal{G})$.
nodes.statement_short: By (16), P_x(y) is not g-identifiable.

nodes.name: Sufficient part
nodes.statement:
\textit{Sufficient part}: 
            Suppose $Q[\mathbf{S}_i]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$ for each $i\in [1:l]$.
            \cite{tian2003ID} showed that 
            \[Q[\mathbf{S}] = \prod_{i=1}^{l}Q[\mathbf{S}_i].\]
            Hence, $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is uniquely computable and therefore, g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
nodes.statement_short: Q[S] is the product of the Q[S_i].

nodes.name: Necessary part
nodes.statement:
\textit{Necessary part}: 
            Suppose $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$. 
            For $i\in [1:l]$, \cite{tian2003ID} provided a formula for computing $Q[\mathbf{S}_i]$ from $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ (Lemma 4, Equations (71) and (72) in \citep{tian2003ID}). 
            Hence, for each $i\in [1:l]$, $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is uniquely computable and therefore, g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
nodes.statement_short: Each Q[S_i] is computable from Q[S] (Tian-Pearl).

nodes.name: Witness models on G'
nodes.statement_short: Take M1', M2' witnessing non-g-identifiability on G'.

nodes.name: Extend to G
nodes.statement_short: Copy conditionals on V' and make other variables constant 0.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
Because variable $V \in \mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{V}'$ can only take value $0$ with probability one, then $Q^{\mathcal{M}_j}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v})=Q^{\mathcal{M}'_j}[\mathbf{A}'_i](\mathbf{v})$ for all $i$ and $Q^{\mathcal{M}_j}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}_0)=Q^{\mathcal{M}_j'}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}_0)$ for $j\in\{1,2\}$. 
        Thus, we have
        \begin{align*}
            &Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}) = Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{A}_i](\mathbf{v}), \quad i\in[0:m],\\
            &Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}_0) \neq Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{v}_0).
        \end{align*}
        This shows that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{G})$.
nodes.statement_short: All Q values coincide with the G' ones, so the models witness non-g-identifiability.

nodes.name: Reduce to positivity
nodes.statement:
By the construction, it is clear that the model belongs to $\mathbb{M}(\mathcal{G}')$. 
        Hence, we need to show that $P(\mathbf{v})>0$ for any $\mathbf{v}\in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$.
nodes.statement_short: Model is in M(G'); need P(v)>0.

nodes.name: Suffices one good u
nodes.statement_short: Enough to find u-hat with P(v,u-hat)>0.

nodes.name: Fix v
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{v}$ be a fixed realization in $\dom{\mathbf{V}'}$. 
        For the rest of the proof, we assume all the realizations for $\mathbf{V}'$ are consistent with $\mathbf{v}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a realization v.

nodes.name: Factorize and reduce to T
nodes.statement:
By Markov factorization property,  for any $\mathbf{u}\in \dom{\mathbf{U}'}$ we have 
        \begin{equation}
            P(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u}) = \prod_{V\in \mathbf{V}'}P(v\mid \Pa{V}{\mathcal{G}'})\prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}'}P(u).
        \end{equation}
        By the construction of our model, we have $P(u)>0$ for any $U\in \mathbf{U}'$ and $u\in \dom{U}$. 
        Moreover, for any $X\in \mathbf{S}$ and any realization for $\Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}'}\cap \mathbf{U}'$ we have $P(x \mid \Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}'})>0$. 
        Hence, it is enough to show that there exists $\hat{\mathbf{u}}\in \dom{\mathbf{U}'}$ such that $P(x \mid \Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}'})>0$ for each $X\in \mathbf{T}$.
nodes.statement_short: U and S factors are positive; only T conditionals matter.

nodes.name: Recall T construction
nodes.statement_short: T coordinates are parities.

nodes.name: Sets U_i
nodes.statement:
By the construction, we define the entries corresponding to each $\mathcal{F}_i$ separately. 
        For each $i\in [0:k]$, let $\mathbf{U}_i$ to be the set of unobserved variables in $\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{T}}$ that are in $\mathcal{F}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Handle each c-forest separately via U_i.

nodes.name: Goal for fixed i
nodes.statement:
Let us fix an $i\in [0:k]$. 
        To finish the prove, we will introduce a method to determine $\hat{u}[i]$ for each $U\in \mathbf{U}_i$ such that 
        \begin{equation} x[i] \equiv \left(\sum_{Y \in \Pa{X}{\mathcal{F}_{i}}} y[i]\right) \pmod{2},
        \end{equation}
        for each $X\in \mathbf{T} \cap \mathbf{B}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose U bits to satisfy the parity equations (18).

nodes.name: Bit-flip trick
nodes.statement:
Lets start with an arbitrary set of values for $\{\hat{u}[i]\!:\: U\in \mathbf{U}_i\}$ which are either $0$ or $1$. 
        Suppose $X\in \mathbf{T} \cap \mathbf{B}_i$. 
        We introduce a trick such that $x[i]$ will be replaced by $1- x[i]$ while for all $Y\in \mathbf{T} \cap \mathbf{B}_i$, $y[i]$ remains the same: \\
        By the construction of $\mathcal{F}_i$, there exists a path $(X=X_1, U_1, X_2, \cdots, X_l,U_l,Z = X_{l+1} )$ from $X$ to a variable $Z \in \mathbf{S}$ such that $\{U_1, \cdots, U_l\} \subseteq \mathbf{U}_i$, $\{X_1,\cdots,X_l\} \subseteq \mathbf{B}_i \cap \mathbf{T}$, and $\Ch{U_j}{\mathcal{F}_i} = \{X_j, X_{j+1}\}$ for each $j\in [1:l]$. 
        Now for each $j \in [1:l]$, we replace $\hat{u}_j[i]$ by $1-\hat{u}_j[i]$. 
        Since Equation \eqref{eq: eq for T} is in mod $2$, the value of $x_j[i]$ will be the same for each $j\in [2:l]$ while $x[i]$ will be replaced by $1-x[i]$. 
        Note that $X_{l+1}=Z \notin \mathbf{T}$.
nodes.statement_short: Flip U bits along a path to S to toggle one T bit.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
With the trick described above, we can construct any realization for the $i$-th bit of the variables in $\mathbf{T} \cap \mathbf{B}_i$. 
        Hence, we can construct $\hat{\mathbf{u}}\in \dom{\mathbf{U}'}$ such that $P(x \mid \Pa{X}{\mathcal{G}'})>0$ for each $X\in \mathbf{T}$.
nodes.statement_short: Any T bit pattern is achievable, giving positive probability.

nodes.name: Consecutive Gamma elements
nodes.statement_short: Fix v and two consecutive elements of Gamma.

nodes.name: Define f_{i,j}
nodes.statement_short: Define the partial sums f over U^S.

nodes.name: Reduce to f
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to show equality of f for each u^T.

nodes.name: T outside B_i
nodes.statement: When $T\in \mathbf{A}'_i\setminus\mathbf{B}_i$, then for fixed realizations of $\textbf{u}^{\mathbf{T}}$,  $P(t|\Pa{T}{\mathcal{G}'})$ is the same for both realizations $\gamma_{l_1}$ and $\gamma_{l_2}$ since $\gamma_{l_1}\equiv\gamma_{l_2}$ mod 2.
nodes.statement_short: These factors agree since the gammas agree mod 2.

nodes.name: Zero T factor
nodes.statement_short: If some T factor vanishes, both f are 0.

nodes.name: Nonzero T factors
nodes.statement:
When $P(t|\Pa{T}{\mathcal{G}'})=1$ for all $T\in \mathbf{B}_i\setminus\mathbf{S}$,
        to prove $f_{i, l_1}(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u}^{\mathbf{T}})=f_{i, l_2}(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u}^{\mathbf{S}})$, we show that for any realization $(\textbf{u}_1,\gamma_{l_1})$ of $(\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}},U_0)$, there is a realization $(\textbf{u}_2,\gamma_{l_2})$  of $(\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}},U_0)$ such that 
        \begin{equation*}
            \prod_{V \in \mathbf{S}} P(v \mid \Pa{V}{\mathcal{G}'})\Big|_{(\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}},U_0)=(\textbf{u}_1,\gamma_{l_1})}=\prod_{V \in \mathbf{S}} P(v \mid \Pa{V}{\mathcal{G}'})\Big|_{(\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}},U_0)=(\textbf{u}_2,\gamma_{l_2})},
        \end{equation*}
        where $P(v \mid \Pa{V}{\mathcal{G}'})\Big|_{(\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}},U_0)=(\textbf{u}_1,\gamma_{l_1})}$ denotes the conditional probability of $v$ given its parents in which the unobserved variables $(\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}},U_0)$ are fixed to be  $(\textbf{u}_1,\gamma_{l_1})$.
        To this end, we consider two cases depending on $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Need a bijection of U^S realizations matching S products.

nodes.name: First case i <= k
nodes.statement_short: Parity forces some I(S)=1; shift U^S along a path.

nodes.name: Parity equation
nodes.statement_short: T bits satisfy the parity equation (20).

nodes.name: Set Lambda
nodes.statement_short: Parents of S outside S have even total parity.

nodes.name: Justify parity
nodes.statement:
This is because, in graph $\mathcal{F}_i$, each observed variable outside of $\mathbf{S}$ has at most one child outside of $\mathbf{S}$, and each unobserved node has either one or two children outside of $\mathbf{S}$. 
        According to (\ref{eq: tmp1}), those unobserved nodes with two children outside of $\mathbf{S}$ do not belong to $\mathbf{\Lambda}\cap \mathbf{U}'$. 
        Such unobserved nodes have exactly two observed descendants in $\mathbf{\Lambda}\cap \mathbf{B}_i$, and because both descendants appear in \eqref{eq: tmp2}, their summation is zero mod 2. 
        On the other hand, the unobserved nodes with only one child outside of $\mathbf{S}$ belong to $\mathbf{\Lambda}\cap \mathbf{U}'$ and have exactly one observed descendant in $\mathbf{\Lambda}\cap \mathbf{B}_i$. Thus, the summation of such unobserved variables and their observed descendant is again zero mod 2 in \eqref{eq: tmp2}.
nodes.statement_short: Count children outside S in the c-forest.

nodes.name: Some I(S)=1
nodes.statement:
If $\mathbb{I}(S)=0$ for all $S \in \mathbf{S}$, then by our model construction, for any variable $W \in \mathbf{\Lambda}\setminus \{T_i\}$, $w[i]$ is an even number but $T_i$ takes value 1 with probability one. 
        Hence, the summation in \eqref{eq: tmp2} cannot be an even number.
        Therefore, there exists at least a variable $S\in \mathbf{S}$ such that $\mathbb{I}(S)=1$. 
        In this case, the value of $P(S|\Pa{S}{\mathcal{G}'})$ does not depend on the realizations of variables in $\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise the parity would be odd.

nodes.name: Bijection claim
nodes.statement_short: Shift values along a bidirected path to match products.

nodes.name: Path from U_0
nodes.statement: Since $\mathcal{G}'_{\mathbf{S}}$ is a c-component, there exists a sequence of variables $U_0, \hat{S}_1, \hat{U}_1, \hat{S}_2, \hat{U}_2, \dots, \hat{U}_l, S$, such that $U_0$ is a parent of $\hat{S}_1$, $S$ is a children of $\hat{U}_l$ and $\hat{U}_j$ is a parent of variables $\hat{S}_j$ and $\hat{S}_{j+1}$ for $j \in [1:l-1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a bidirected path from U_0 to S.

nodes.name: Alternating shift
nodes.statement_short: Shift by +-2 alternately; this bijection gives (22).

nodes.name: Second case i > k
nodes.statement_short: Path to a node of S outside A_i' and the same shift.

nodes.name: S not in A_i'
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Second case, when $i \in [k+1:m]$:} 
        In this case, $\mathbf{S} \setminus \mathbf{A}_i'\neq \varnothing$.
nodes.statement_short: Some S lies outside A_i'.

nodes.name: Path to S outside A_i'
nodes.statement: Since $\mathcal{G}'_{\mathbf{S}}$ is a c-component, there exists a sequence of variables $U_0, \hat{S}_1, \hat{U}_1, \hat{S}_2, \hat{U}_2, \dots, \hat{U}_l, S$, such that $U_0$ is a parent of $\hat{S}_1$, $S\in \mathbf{S}\setminus \mathbf{A}_i'$ is a children of $\hat{U}_l$ and $\hat{U}_j$ is a parent of variables $\hat{S}_j$ and  $\hat{S}_{j+1}$ for $j \in [1:l-1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Bidirected path from U_0 to S not in A_i'.

nodes.name: Same shift
nodes.statement_short: Same alternating shift yields (22).

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Herein, we proved that $\theta_{i, l_1}(\mathbf{v})=\theta_{i, l_2}(\mathbf{v})$. By varying $x$ within $[0 : \frac{\kappa-1}{2}]$ in the definition of $\gamma_{l_1}$ and $\gamma_{l_2}$, we  conclude the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Vary x over Gamma to get the lemma.

nodes.name: Choose r, t
nodes.statement_short: Compare gamma = (0,...) and (2,...).

nodes.name: Choose v_0
nodes.statement:
We choose $\textbf{v}_0$ as follows: set all variables in $\mathbf{S}$ to be zero and select a realization for variables in $\mathbf{V}' \setminus \mathbf{S}$ such that $\mathbb{I}(S)=0$ for all $S \in \mathbf{S}$. 
        Denote by $S_0$ a child of $U_0$ in $\mathbf{S}$.
nodes.statement_short: Set S to 0 and pick T values with all I(S)=0.

nodes.name: eta_r has a large term
nodes.statement: Note that there is a term in the summation of the right side of equation (\ref{eq: tmp4.1}) that is $(1-\kappa\epsilon)^{|\mathbf{S}|}$. For instance, this occurs when all realizations of unobserved variables in $\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}$ are zero.
nodes.statement_short: eta_r contains a (1-kappa eps)^{|S|} term.

nodes.name: eta_t terms have eps factor
nodes.statement_short: No U^S realization makes all S factors large when U_0 = gamma_t.

nodes.name: Reformulate
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to show the congruences have no solution.

nodes.name: Two-colouring
nodes.statement:
Suppose there is a realization of $\mathbf{U}^{\mathbf{S}}$ such that the above equations hold. In this case, since $\mathcal{G}'_{\mathbf{S}}$ is a tree, we can color its nodes with two colors, red and black, such that connected nodes by biderected edges have different colors. 
        Suppose that $\mathbf{S}_1$ is the set of black variables and $\mathbf{S}_2$ is the set of red variables which (without loss of generality) contains $S_0 \in \mathbf{S}_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a solution and two-colour the tree G'_S.

nodes.name: Parity contradiction
nodes.statement_short: Summing per colour class gives incompatible congruences.

nodes.name: Every term has eps
nodes.statement: Hence, in Equation \eqref{eq: tmp4.2}, there exists a term in the summation with probability $\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Each term of eta_t has an eps factor.

nodes.name: Polynomial argument
nodes.statement:
Therefore, in extreme case, when $\epsilon=0$, $\eta_{t}(\mathbf{v}')=0$. However, 
        $\eta_{r}(\mathbf{v}')\geq (1-\kappa\epsilon)^{|\mathbf{S}|}\prod_{U\in \mathbf{U}'\setminus \{U_0\}}\! P(u)>0$. 
        Since $\eta_{r}(v)$ and $\eta_{t}(v)$ are polynomial functions of $\epsilon$ and they are not equal at $\epsilon=0$, then there exists a small enough $0<\epsilon<\frac{1}{\kappa}$ such that $\eta_{r}(\mathbf{v}') \neq \eta_{t}(\mathbf{v}')$.
nodes.statement_short: At eps=0 they differ, so for small eps they differ.

nodes.name: Scope
nodes.statement: In this section, we provide our proof for the necessary part of Theorem \ref{thm: main} when $\mathbf{S}\nsubseteq \mathbf{A}_i'$ for all $i\in [0:m]$.
nodes.statement_short: Treat the case where S is in no A_i.
nodes.section: C A special case in the proof of Theorem thm: main

nodes.name: Reduce graph to F^S
nodes.statement:
We define $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}$ to be a minimal (in terms of edges) spanning subgraph of $\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{S}]$ such that $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{S}}$ is a single c-component. 
    In this case, we can assume $\mathbf{V}' = \mathbf{S}$, $\mathcal{G}'$ is $\mathcal{F}^{\mathbf{S}}$, and $\mathbb{A}'= \{\mathbf{A}_i':=\mathbf{A}_i \cap \mathbf{V}'\}_{i=0}^m$. 
    For each $i\in [0:m]$, we have $\mathbf{A}_i' \subsetneq \mathbf{V}'$.
nodes.statement_short: Take G' = F^S, V' = S.
nodes.section: C A special case in the proof of Theorem thm: main

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2
nodes.statement:
Note that Lemma \ref{lem: simplify} holds for this case. 
    Hence, it is enough to show that $Q[\mathbf{S}]$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}', \mathcal{G}')$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to work on (A', G').
nodes.section: C A special case in the proof of Theorem thm: main

nodes.name: Restate setting
nodes.statement:
Recall that our assumptions and goal in this section are as follows:\\
    $\mathcal{G}'$ is a DAG with observed variables $\mathbf{V}'$ and unobserved variables $\mathbf{U}'$ such that $\mathcal{G}'_{\mathbf{V}'}$ has no directed edges and its bidirected edges form a spanning tree over $\mathbf{V}'$. 
    $\mathbb{A}'= \{\mathbf{A}_i'\}_{i=0}^m$ is a collection of subsets such that $\mathbf{A}_i' \subsetneq \mathbf{V}'$. 
    The goal is to show that $Q[\mathbf{V}']$ is not g-identifiable from $(\mathbb{A}',\mathcal{G}')$.
nodes.statement_short: G'_V' is a bidirected spanning tree; all A_i' are proper.
nodes.section: C A special case in the proof of Theorem thm: main

nodes.name: Goal models
nodes.statement_short: Need models agreeing on Q[A_i'] but differing on Q[S].
nodes.section: C A special case in the proof of Theorem thm: main

nodes.name: Binary domains
nodes.statement:
For both models $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$ we define each observed and unobserved variable to be binary, i.e $\dom{W}=\{0, 1\}$ for all $W \in \mathbf{V}' \cup \mathbf{U}'$.
    Next, we define the equation of the variables in each model.
nodes.statement_short: All variables binary.
nodes.section: C A special case in the proof of Theorem thm: main

nodes.name: Model 1
nodes.statement_short: Each V is the XOR of its parents with prob 1-eps, else uniform.

nodes.name: Private parents
nodes.statement: Suppose $\mathbf{A}_i':= \{A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n\}$. Since $\mathbf{A}_i' \subsetneq \mathbf{V}'$, there are distinct unobserved variables $U_1, U_2, \dots, U_n$, such that $U_j$ is a parent of the $A_j$ for $j \in [1: n]$. Denote by $\mathcal{M}$ any of the model $\mathcal{M}_1$ or $\mathcal{M}_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Each A_j has a distinct unobserved parent U_j.

nodes.name: U_j determined
nodes.statement_short: XOR equations determine U_1..U_t uniquely.

nodes.statement_short: Summing gives 2^{-n}.

nodes.name: Position independence goal
nodes.statement: Define  $n=|\mathbf{V}'|$ and $\mathbf{V}' = \{V_1, V_2, \dots, V_n\}$. Firstly, we will prove that for any $\mathbf{v} \in \dom{\mathbf{V}'}$, the value of $Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{V}'](\mathbf{v})$ does not depend on the position of $V_1$ in graph $\mathcal{G}'$.
nodes.statement_short: First show Q^{M2} does not depend on where V_1 is.
nodes.section: C A special case in the proof of Theorem thm: main

nodes.name: Swap negation to neighbour
nodes.statement:
Denote by $V_2$ an observed variable which is connected to the $V_1$ by a bidirected edge in $\mathcal{G}'_{\mathbf{V}'}$.
        Let $U$ denotes the unobserved variable (corresponding to the bidirected edge) which is a parent of $V_1$ and $V_2$. 
        Next, we define a new model $\mathcal{M}_2'$ in which all variables in $\mathbf{V}'$ are defined similarly as they are defined in model $\mathcal{M}_2$ except for variables $V_1$ and $V_2$. 
        In $\mathcal{M}_2'$, we define $V_2$ in the same way as $V_1$ is defined in  $\mathcal{M}_2$.
        We also define $V_1$ in $\mathcal{M}_2'$ in the same way as $V_2$ is defined in $\mathcal{M}_2$.
        Then, we have
        \begin{align*}
            \prod_{i=1}^n P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(v_i|\Pa{V_i}{\mathcal{G}'}) = P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(v_1|\Pa{V_1}{\mathcal{G}'})P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(v_2|\Pa{V_2}{\mathcal{G}'})\prod_{i=3}^{n}P(v_i|\Pa{V_i}{\mathcal{G}'}) \\
            = P^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(v_1|\Pa{V_1}{\mathcal{G}'}\setminus\{U\}, u\oplus 1)P^{\mathcal{M}_2'}(v_2|\Pa{V_2}{\mathcal{G}'}\setminus\{U\}, u\oplus 1)\prod_{i=3}^{n}P(v_i|\Pa{V_i}{\mathcal{G}'}).
        \end{align*}
        This implies that substituting $V_1$ by $V_2$ does not change the value of $Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{V}'](\mathbf{v})$.
nodes.statement_short: Flipping the shared U moves the negation to a neighbour.
nodes.section: C A special case in the proof of Theorem thm: main

nodes.name: WLOG V_1 a leaf
nodes.statement:
Without loss of generality, suppose that $V_1$ is a leaf in $\mathcal{G}'$ and $U_1$ is a parent of $V_1$. Note that there are exactly $n-1$ unobserved variables in graph $\mathcal{G}'$.
        This is because $\mathcal{G}'_{\mathbf{V}'}$ is a tree with bidirected edges over $\mathbf{V}'$. Therefore, we have
        \begin{align*}
            & 2^{n-1}Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{V}'](\mathbf{0}) = P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(V_1=0|U_1=0)\!\! \sum_{\mathbf{U}' \setminus \{ U_1\}} \prod_{j>1}P(v_j|\Pa{V_j}{\mathcal{G}'}) + P^{\mathcal{M}_1}(V_1=0|U_1=1)\!\! \sum_{\mathbf{U}' \setminus \{ U_1\}} \prod_{j>1}P(v_j|\Pa{V_j}{\mathcal{G}'}), \\
            & 2^{n-1}Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{V}'](\mathbf{0}) = P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(V_1=0|U_1=0)\!\! \sum_{\mathbf{U}' \setminus \{ U_1\}} \prod_{j>1}P(v_j|\Pa{V_j}{\mathcal{G}'}) + P^{\mathcal{M}_2}(V_1=0|U_1=1)\!\! \sum_{\mathbf{U}' \setminus \{ U_1\}} \prod_{j>1}P(v_j|\Pa{V_j}{\mathcal{G}'}).
        \end{align*}
        Note that:
nodes.statement_short: Expand Q at 0 over U_1.

nodes.name: Reduce to a != b
nodes.statement_short: Q values are mixtures of a and b with swapped weights.
nodes.section: C A special case in the proof of Theorem thm: main

nodes.name: Smaller models
nodes.statement:
Denote by $S_n$ an observed variable connected to the $V_1$ by a bidirect edge in $\mathcal{G}'_{\mathbf{\mathbf{V}'}}$.
        We define $\mathbf{V}'_{n-1} := \mathbf{V}'\setminus \{V_1\}$, $\mathbf{U}'_{n-1} := \mathbf{U}'\setminus \{U_1\}$ and $\mathcal{G}_{n-1}:=\mathcal{G}'[\mathbf{V}' \setminus \{V_1\}]$.
        We also define models $\mathcal{M}_1^{(n-1)}$ and $\mathcal{M}_2^{(n-1)}$ as follows:
nodes.statement_short: Define reduced graph and models on n-1 nodes.
nodes.section: C A special case in the proof of Theorem thm: main

nodes.name: New model M1^(n-1)
nodes.statement_short: XOR model on G_{n-1}.
nodes.section: C A special case in the proof of Theorem thm: main

nodes.name: Model M2^(n-1)
nodes.statement_short: Negated XOR at S_n.
nodes.section: C A special case in the proof of Theorem thm: main

nodes.name: a, b as smaller Q values
nodes.statement:
Note that:
        \begin{align*}
            & \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^{n-2}\sum_{U_1=0, \mathbf{U}'_{n-1}} \prod_{j>1}P(V_j|\Pa{V_j}{\mathcal{G}'}) =   \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^{n-2}a = Q^{\mathcal{M}_1^{(n-1)}}[\mathbf{V}'_{n-1}](\mathbf{0}),\\
            & \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^{n-2}\sum_{U_1=1, \mathbf{U}'_{n-1}} \prod_{j>1}P(V_j|\Pa{V_j}{\mathcal{G}'}) =   \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^{n-2}b =   Q^{\mathcal{M}_2^{(n-1)}}[\mathbf{V}'_{n-1}](\mathbf{0}).
        \end{align*}
        It remains to show  $Q^{\mathcal{M}_1^{(n-1)}}[\mathbf{V}'_{n-1}](\mathbf{0})\neq Q^{\mathcal{M}_2^{(n-1)}}[\mathbf{V}'_{n-1}](\mathbf{0})$. 
        Note that if this holds, then by our construction, $Q^{\mathcal{M}_1}[\mathbf{V}'](\mathbf{0})\neq Q^{\mathcal{M}_2}[\mathbf{V}'](\mathbf{0})$.
